Through Underscore Marketing, a US agency, I also worked on oncology, rare disease and gene therapy brands.

Two or more platforms under one operator and one measurement layer is PPC management. Agencies that need a senior operator on a client account: white label PPC.

## Who this fits

### Companies spending $3K to $80K a month

Enough for the flat fee to be a small share of the total, and small enough that one senior person can run everything properly. Below that, a setup or audit is the better buy.

### Owners and marketing leads who want the operator

You would rather talk to the person in the account than to someone relaying their questions. Reports are written for owners: cost per customer and what changed.

Home services, healthcare, B2B and SaaS, law firms and professional services, online stores. More industry pages are on diwizi.com.

## How an engagement starts

- A short form. Spend band, site and what has been tried. I reply myself with whether it is a fit, what I would look at first and a price range; a short call follows if it makes sense.

- A fixed-price audit. Written findings ranked by impact: tracking first, then structure, then bidding and search terms. Yours to implement, with or without me.

- Build or rebuild. Tracking fixed before anything else, because every bidding decision inherits whatever the conversion data says.

- Month-to-month management. Weekly work in the account, a written monthly report, a call whenever you want one. Thirty days' notice instead of a contract term.

## Freelance specialist, agency or in-house: which fits your account

| | Freelance specialist | Agency | In-house hire |

| Who touches the account | The person you hired | Whoever has capacity | The person you hired |

| Typical cost | Flat retainer | Retainer or % of spend, with minimums | Salary, benefits, tools, ramp-up |

| Best for | $3K to $80K monthly spend, one or a few markets | Many markets and channels, creative at volume | Spend large enough to justify a full-time role |

| Weak spot | Capacity: one person cannot run forty accounts | Turnover on the account team | One account is the whole job |

I keep the client list short on purpose; that is what makes the first column work. What a month with a freelance PPC consultant looks like, and how it differs from an agency retainer, is on its own page.

### FAQ

**How much does a Google Ads freelancer cost?** Management is a flat monthly fee set by scope, not tied to ad spend. An audit is a fixed price quoted from the form and credited against the first month if you continue. No twelve-month contract. The pricing page explains how each model behaves and what to ask before you sign with anyone.

**What is the minimum ad spend you work with?** No hard minimum, but the retainer only makes sense once the account spends enough for the fee to be a small share of the total; in practice from about $3,000 a month. Below that, a one-off setup or audit is the better buy.

**Who owns the Google Ads account, the tags and the landing pages?** You do, always. I work inside your accounts with manager access. Nothing is built in a container I control, so leaving me never means starting over.

**Do you work with clients outside the United States?** Yes. The site is written for the US, Canada and Europe, and I work with companies from any country that operate in English, quoted in US dollars, pounds or euros. UK and Irish businesses also have ppcconsultancy.uk, quoted in pounds for the UK and euros for Ireland. I work remotely from Curitiba, Brazil, on GMT-3 all year: one to five hours ahead of US time zones, depending on the zone and the season, and three to five hours behind Europe, so calls fit a US morning or a European afternoon.

**Can you take over an account an agency built?** Yes, and it is one of the most common starting points. The audit usually finds duplicated conversion actions, broad match on Smart Bidding without negatives, and campaigns organised by whoever built them rather than by what you sell.

**Do you also run Meta or Microsoft Ads?** Yes. Google Ads is the core of the work, and Meta Ads and Microsoft Advertising are added when there is a measured reason, run by the same person.

## PPC Consultant | Independent Freelance PPC Consultant, US, Canada, Europe

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/freelance-ppc-consultant/
Description: Independent PPC consultant with 14+ years in Google Ads, Microsoft Advertising and Meta Ads. Hired directly, month to month, for a flat fee.

I am Diego Willian Zietek, an independent PPC consultant for companies in the United States, Canada and Europe. I audit, plan and run the accounts myself: Google Ads first, Microsoft Advertising and Meta Ads where they earn their place, with tracking done by the same person.

## What a PPC consultant covers

PPC is broader than Google Ads. A PPC consultant plans and runs paid search across Google and Microsoft, and often the paid social that sits next to it, with one account structure, one measurement layer and one person accountable for the result. That last part is what people are usually buying when they look for a PPC consultant rather than an agency: direct access to whoever does the work.

### Paid search

Google Ads Search, Shopping and Performance Max, plus Microsoft Advertising, which in the US still delivers a cheaper click on the same intent for many B2B and finance accounts.

### Paid social

Meta Ads for demand and remarketing. Run only when there is a reason, not because the invoice looks fuller.

### Measurement

GA4, Google Tag Manager, consent mode and offline conversion import, so the platforms optimize toward customers rather than form fills. See conversion tracking.

## PPC consultant or PPC agency

Agencies are the right answer for some accounts: many markets, many languages, a creative pipeline that needs a team. For a single company spending between a few thousand and a hundred thousand dollars a month, the agency structure mostly adds cost and distance. Three differences matter in practice.

- Who does the work. With an independent consultant this should be a trivial question with one answer. If it is not, you are talking to a small agency describing itself as a consultant.

- How pricing bends behavior. A percentage of spend rewards spend. A flat fee rewards keeping the client. I charge a flat monthly fee for PPC management, agreed up front and reviewed when scope changes.

- What happens when you leave. Everything I build sits in your own Google Ads, Microsoft Advertising, Meta and analytics accounts. That is worth settling in writing with anyone you hire, me included.

## What a month with a PPC consultant looks like

- Weekly, in the account. Search terms reviewed and negatives added, bids and budgets adjusted against the target, ads and assets rotated when a test has a winner, feed or landing page issues flagged to whoever owns them.

- Monthly, in writing. Cost per lead or per customer, what changed, what I plan to change next, and what I need from you. Written for the owner, not for another marketer.

- Quarterly, at the structure. Are the campaigns still organized the way the business makes decisions: by service line, margin and geography? Structures drift as accounts grow, and a quarterly rebuild of the weak parts is cheaper than a yearly rescue.

How the first look at an account goes, check by check, is in a worked audit example.

## Working with companies in the US, Canada and Europe

I work remotely from Brazil, in English and mostly in writing. Brazil sits one to two hours ahead of US Eastern time, so calls fit comfortably into a US morning or early afternoon, and written replies come within one working day. Reporting is in dollars, and everything is built in your own accounts from the first day.

Based in the UK or Ireland? The same practice runs a UK site with prices in pounds: ppcconsultancy.uk. And if you are a PPC specialist looking for contract work, this is not a vacancy; accounts are not passed on to subcontractors.

## Consultant, contractor or freelancer

Some companies search for a PPC contractor: a specialist hired on a contract for a defined period or scope rather than on an open-ended retainer. The terms here fit that. Management runs month to month with 30 days' notice either way, so a contract of three or six months is simply the same engagement with an end date written in. Project work (an audit, a setup, a tracking rebuild, a set of landing pages) is a fixed price with a defined deliverable. Either way you contract directly with me, not with an agency that assigns someone.

## What the work has produced

For Trutek, a Brazilian truck parts company, the Google Ads account I have run since 2020 shows about 260 attributed contact conversions from 5,707 clicks. For a health plan reseller, Google Ads produced 651 quote requests in October 2019 at R$ 14.31 each, on the same spend as the month before. The method is not exotic: campaigns split by intent, tracking that separates a real enquiry from noise, a weekly pass through the search terms and steady tests of ads and pages. The results page lays out the published engagements and what can and cannot be verified.

### FAQ

**Can I hire you as a PPC contractor for a fixed period?** Yes. A three- or six-month contract is the same month-to-month engagement with an end date written in, and project work is a fixed price with a defined deliverable. You contract directly with me.

**What does a PPC consultant do?** Audits the accounts, decides what to fix first, and then either advises your team or runs the campaigns directly: search terms, bids, budgets, ads, landing pages and the tracking underneath. With an independent consultant, the same person does all of it.

**Is a PPC consultant the same as a PPC freelancer?** Mostly the label. Both are one independent person. "Consultant" leans toward strategy and advice, "freelancer" toward hands-on work in the account. I do both: the audit and the plan, then the weekly work that carries it out.

**What does a PPC consultant charge?** Either a fixed price for a defined piece of work, such as an audit or a rebuild, or a flat monthly retainer for ongoing management. I do not charge a percentage of ad spend. Fees are quoted once I know the account size and platforms, usually from the form alone; the pricing page explains the models.

**Is a PPC consultant right for a small business?** If the business spends enough for the fee to be a sensible share of the total, yes. Below roughly $3,000 a month, an audit plus a one-off setup that you then run yourself is usually better value than a retainer. The small business page goes into it.

**Can one consultant really cover Google, Microsoft and Meta?** For a single company, yes, and it is better that way: one measurement layer and one person deciding where the next dollar goes. What one person cannot do is produce creative at agency volume, so for Meta-heavy brands I work alongside your designer or a creative studio rather than replacing them.

**Do you sign a contract?** A short agreement covering scope, fee, confidentiality and that everything built belongs to you. It is month to month, with 30 days' notice rather than a fixed term.

**How quickly can you start?** An audit usually starts within a week of the go-ahead. Ongoing management depends on capacity, because I deliberately keep the client list short; if I cannot take the account on properly, I will say so on the call.

**Do you work with agencies?** Yes, as a senior operator brought in on specific accounts, usually white label. That is described on the white label PPC page.

## Google Ads Consultant | Independent Google Ads Consulting & Strategy

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/google-ads-consultant/
Description: Independent Google Ads consultant for companies and in-house teams: strategy, second opinions, coaching and hands-on fixes. 14+ years, no agency layer.

Consulting for companies that run Google Ads in-house or through an agency and want someone with no stake in the retainer to look at the account, set the strategy, or fix the parts nobody owns.

## What a Google Ads consultant does that a manager does not

Management is the weekly work inside the account. Consulting is the layer above it: deciding what the account is for, how it should be structured, what to measure, and whether the people running it are doing the right things. Most companies buy management and get no consulting, because the person running the account has neither the seniority nor the incentive to question the setup they inherited.

I offer Google Ads consulting in three shapes. All of them are delivered by me, in writing and on calls, and none of them require you to move the account.

### Strategy and structure

How budget should split across Search, Shopping, Performance Max and YouTube; how campaigns should map to margin, service line and geography; what a realistic cost per customer is given your auction. Delivered as a written plan your team or agency can execute.

### Second opinion on an agency or freelancer

You suspect the account is under-managed but cannot prove it. I review the account, the reporting and the invoices, and tell you plainly what is being done well, what is not, and what to ask for. The audit is the formal version of this.

### Advisory for in-house teams

A standing monthly or fortnightly session with the person who runs your ads: reviewing changes, unblocking decisions, and building the judgement that courses do not teach. Often called Google Ads coaching; it is closer to a fractional head of paid search.

## The problems that usually bring someone to a consultant

- The numbers do not agree. Google Ads reports one conversion count, GA4 another, the CRM a third, and nobody will say which one is real. Until that is fixed, every optimisation decision is built on sand. This is where I start, every time.

- Clicks are cheaper and leads are worse. The account is being optimised towards a metric that is easy to move rather than the one that pays the bills. Usually a conversion action problem, sometimes a bidding strategy problem, occasionally both.

- Spend went up and revenue did not. Broad match and Performance Max expand happily into demand you were already capturing for free, including your own brand. Exclusions and structure fix it; more budget does not.

- The agency report is three pages of green arrows. Impressions up, CTR up, CPC down, and the sales team quietly hiring a second SDR to qualify the leads. A consultant with no retainer to protect reads that report differently.

- A new market, product or platform. Launching in Canada or the UK, adding Shopping, moving from lead forms to booked calls. The decisions made in the first month set the cost base for the next year.

## How consulting is priced and delivered

Consulting is either a fixed-price piece of work with a defined deliverable, or an hourly advisory arrangement for teams that want a standing session. Hourly is the right model here and the wrong model for ongoing management, because for management it makes you hesitate before asking a question, which is exactly when accounts drift. The pricing page covers the reasoning.

- Scoping. The form, then a short call if needed, to understand the account, who runs it and what decision you are trying to make.

- Access and review. Read-only access to Google Ads, GA4 and Tag Manager. I read the account the way an auditor reads a ledger: search terms, conversion actions, change history, invoices.

- Written deliverable. A document, not a slide deck. Findings ranked by financial impact, each with the fix, who should do it and how to check it worked.

- Walkthrough and follow-up. One call to go through it with you or your team, and a check-in a month later to see what moved.

## Consulting across platforms

Google Ads is where most of the money and most of the mistakes are, but the same questions apply to Meta Ads and Microsoft Advertising, and to the split between them. A paid search consultant who has never run paid social will always recommend more paid search. I run all three, which makes the budget allocation advice worth something. When the need is hands-on work every week rather than advice, the freelance PPC consultant page describes that engagement.

### FAQ

**What is the difference between a Google Ads consultant and a Google Ads manager?** A manager does the weekly work inside the account. A consultant decides what the account should be doing, checks whether it is, and advises the people who run it. I do both, but consulting can be bought on its own without moving the account.

**Can you consult on an account my agency runs, without replacing them?** Yes, and it often makes the agency relationship better, because you arrive at the next review with specific questions. I will tell you if the agency is doing a good job; plenty are, and I have no retainer to win by saying otherwise.

**Do you offer Google Ads coaching or training?** Yes, as recurring advisory sessions with the person or small team running your ads. It is practical and account-specific rather than a course: we work on your campaigns, your reports and your decisions.

**How much does Google Ads consulting cost?** Fixed price for defined deliverables such as a strategy document or an audit, hourly for standing advisory. Both are quoted after scoping. See the pricing page for how each model behaves.

**Do you need edit access to consult?** No. Read-only access to Google Ads, GA4 and Tag Manager is enough for the review. Edit access only matters if you want me to implement the fixes, which is a separate decision.

**Can I book a single session instead of an engagement?** Yes. A Google Ads consultation is one working session of about an hour on your account, with written notes within two working days, at a fixed price credited against an audit or management if either follows within 60 days.

**Is a consultant worth it for a small account?** For accounts under a few thousand a month, a single fixed-price audit is the sensible way to buy consulting: one document, one walkthrough, then you or your team implement. Ongoing advisory is for teams with enough spend that a better decision each month pays for the session.

## Google Ads Audit | Independent PPC Account Audit, Fixed Price

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/google-ads-audit/
Description: A paid, independent Google Ads audit of tracking, search terms, structure, bidding and Performance Max, with fixes ranked by impact in a report you keep.

Most free PPC audits are sales documents: they find enough problems to justify a proposal and stop. This is a paid, fixed-scope account audit that ends with a prioritised list of fixes you own, whether or not you ever hire me again.

## What a PPC audit usually uncovers

Different companies, different industries, and the same short list of problems. These are the ones that show up in most Google Ads audits I run, roughly in order of how much money they waste.

### Conversions counted more than once

The same lead fires as a form submission, a thank-you pageview and a phone call. Your reported cost per lead is fiction, and Smart Bidding has been optimising towards the fiction for months.

### Search terms nobody has read

In neglected accounts, a double-digit share of budget routinely goes to queries that will never convert: job seekers, students, competitors' brand names, the wrong country.

### Structure built for the tool

Campaigns organised by match type or by whoever built them, instead of by margin, service line and geography, which is what you actually make decisions on.

### Automation on defaults

Broad match with Smart Bidding and no negatives. Performance Max with no brand exclusion, quietly buying demand you already had. Auto-applied recommendations switched on.

### Budget where the margin is not

The cheapest service to sell receives the most budget because it produces the most conversions, while the profitable one is capped. Correct by the platform's logic, wrong by yours.

### Landing pages that leak

Ads promising one thing, pages offering another; forms that fail on mobile; call buttons that are not tracked. The account can be perfect and still lose here.

## What the audit covers

- Measurement first. Every conversion action, its source, its counting method and its attribution setting. GA4 and Tag Manager configuration. Consent mode. Whether the numbers in Google Ads can be reconciled with the CRM. If this layer is wrong, nothing below it can be trusted, so it is checked before anything else.

- Search terms and negatives. Twelve months of search terms, with the last 90 days read line by line, against the negatives that exist, with the waste quantified. An estimate of the spend that produced nothing. Negative lists proposed by campaign and shared.

- Structure and settings. Campaign and ad group organisation against the business, location and language settings, network settings, ad schedules, device adjustments, and the change history that explains how the account got here.

- Bidding and budgets. Strategy per campaign against its data volume, target settings, budget-limited campaigns that should not be and unlimited ones that should, portfolio strategies and their side effects.

- Ads, assets and Performance Max. Ad strength as a symptom rather than a goal, asset coverage, brand exclusions, asset group logic, feed quality for Shopping.

- Landing pages and conversion path. Message match, speed on mobile, form and call tracking, what happens after the lead arrives.

A worked example on an illustrative account shows the checks in order and what the verdict looks like. The deliverable is a written document with findings ranked by financial impact, each with the fix, who should do it and how to confirm it worked, plus a short call to walk through it. Accounts on Microsoft Advertising or Meta can be added to the same audit; see PPC management and Meta Ads.

## Why the audit is paid

A free audit has to be paid for somehow, and it is paid for by the retainer it is designed to sell. That shapes what it finds. A paid audit can say "the account is in decent shape, fix these three things and keep your current setup", and I have written exactly that more than once. Many clients take the audit, implement it themselves or with their existing team, and never hire me for management. That is a good outcome, not a failed sale.

The price is fixed for your account and set from three things: monthly spend, the number of campaigns, and how many platforms are in scope. Send the form and you get the figure by email within one working day, without a call, and it is credited in full against the first month if management follows. It is the same price whether or not you go on to work with me.

### FAQ

**How much does a Google Ads audit cost?** The price is fixed for your account and set from three things: monthly spend, the number of campaigns, and how many platforms are in scope. Send the form and you get the figure by email within one working day, without a call, and it is credited in full against the first month if management follows. See pricing for the models.

**How long does a PPC audit take?** Five to seven working days from receiving access, for a typical single-platform account. Larger or multi-platform accounts take longer and the quote says so up front.

**What access do you need?** Read-only access to Google Ads, GA4 and Google Tag Manager, and ideally a CRM export or a conversation with whoever handles the leads. I do not change anything during an audit.

**Do I have to hire you afterwards?** No. The report is yours to implement however you like. A meaningful share of audit clients implement it in-house and that is fine.

**Can you audit Meta Ads or Microsoft Advertising too?** Yes. Each platform adds scope and a bit of time, and it is worth doing them together because the tracking layer is shared.

**Will you tell me if my agency is doing a good job?** Yes, in writing. I have no retainer to win by criticising them, and a fair audit that confirms the agency is competent is still useful: it tells you where the remaining gains are.

## Google Ads Freelancer Pricing & PPC Consultant Rates Explained

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/pricing/
Description: What PPC consultants and Google Ads freelancers charge: percentage of spend, flat retainer and hourly compared, and how I price audits and management.

The three ways this industry charges and where each one quietly works against you, what the market typically costs, and how I price audits, management and consulting.

## The three models, and the catch in each

### Percentage of ad spend

Typically 10% to 20% of monthly spend, often with a minimum. Easy to understand, and the incentive runs backwards: the consultant earns more when you spend more, not when you spend better. Watch what happens when the honest advice is to cut budget.

### Flat monthly retainer

A fixed fee regardless of spend. Incentives are cleaner and budgeting is predictable. The risk is scope: if landing pages, tracking or reporting sit outside the retainer, the recommendations you need most never get implemented.

### Hourly

Rates vary enormously with seniority and market. Fine for audits and advisory. Bad for ongoing management, because you start hesitating before asking a question, which is exactly when accounts drift.

The number nobody quotes: whatever the model, ask what happens to the account if you leave. If the campaigns, conversion actions and tags live in the vendor's accounts rather than yours, the real price is that you cannot go.

## What freelance Google Ads management typically costs

Ranges observed across the US and UK markets, for context rather than as a quote. Freelancer rates cluster lower than agency rates for the same spend because there is no account manager, office or margin stack in between; senior freelancers sit at the top of the freelance range and overlap with small agencies.

| Monthly ad spend | Freelance specialist | Small agency | Notes |

| Under $3,000 | One-off setup or audit | Usually below minimums | A retainer rarely makes sense here |

| $3,000 – $10,000 | Flat retainer, set by scope | Minimum retainer or 15–20% of spend | Where the freelance model is strongest |

| $10,000 – $50,000 | Flat retainer, scaled by scope | 10–15% of spend | Percentage models start to overcharge here |

| Over $50,000 | Flat retainer, fractional lead | Custom, often 8–12% ($4,000–6,000+) | Structure and measurement matter more than bids |

Hourly consulting from senior practitioners runs from roughly $100 to $300 an hour depending on market; freelance marketplaces list much lower rates, mostly from people early in their careers or in lower-cost regions.

## How I price

Every engagement is quoted from the form, in US dollars, pounds or euros, because the scope decides the number: monthly spend, number of platforms and markets, and whether tracking has to be rebuilt. What you can rely on before the call is the model. How a month with a freelance PPC consultant runs, compared with an agency retainer, is on its own page.

Landing pages, business websites and tracking setups are the exception: fixed price projects, quoted on request in US dollars, pounds or euros, with the scope in writing before any work starts, half on approval and half on delivery.

The fee is set for your account, not from a rate card: platforms, markets, campaigns and how much landing page and tracking work is included. A range comes by email from the form; a firm figure needs a look at the accounts.

| Engagement | Model | What is included |

| Google Ads audit | Fixed price for your account, set from monthly spend, number of campaigns and platforms in scope | Written report, fixes ranked by impact, walkthrough call. The figure comes by email from the form within one working day and is credited in full against the first month if management follows. |

| Management, up to ~$10K/month spend | Flat monthly fee | Weekly work, tracking maintained, landing page fixes, written monthly report. Month to month. |

| Management, $10K to $50K/month spend | Flat monthly fee, scaled by scope | Same scope with more campaigns, markets or platforms. |

| Management, over $50K/month spend | Flat monthly fee, quoted per account | Multiple platforms and markets, weekly call, a fractional head of paid media rather than an operator. |

| Account setup | Fixed price | Structure, ads, negatives, tracking, launch and handover document. |

| Conversion tracking rebuild | Fixed price | GA4, Tag Manager, enhanced and offline conversions, reconciliation report. |

| Consulting and advisory | Hourly, or fixed price per deliverable | Strategy, second opinions and standing sessions with in-house teams. |

| White label, per client account | Flat monthly fee per account | Volume pricing for several accounts. Your brand, your template. |

None of these is a percentage of ad spend, so the advice to cut budget costs me nothing to give. Adding Microsoft Advertising to a Google retainer is a small increase; adding Meta with weekly creative testing is a larger one, agreed up front. The form asks for exactly that and you get a range back within one working day, often the same day; a firm number needs a look at the account.

## What is not in the price

Ad spend is paid by you, directly to Google, Microsoft or Meta, from your own billing profile. Paid tools beyond what the platforms provide are rare and agreed first. Creative production at volume, for Meta-heavy accounts, is done with your designer or a studio and billed by them. Everything else that the account needs to perform, including tracking fixes and landing page changes I can make myself, is inside the retainer.

### FAQ

**Why not charge a percentage of ad spend like most agencies?** Because it pays the consultant to grow spend rather than results. A flat fee removes that conflict. When the right advice is to cut budget, I can give it without cutting my own income.

**Is there a setup fee?** Starting management has no onboarding fee. Existing accounts start with an audit and new accounts with a setup; either one is a fixed price and is credited against the first month of management.

**Is there a minimum contract length?** No. Management is month to month, with 30 days' notice either way. Accounts need a few months to show what a change did, and most clients stay well beyond that, but the choice is theirs each month.

**Can either side end it?** Either side can end management with 30 days' written notice. Everything stays in your accounts, so nothing has to be migrated when it ends.

**Do you charge more for multiple platforms?** Scope, not platform count, sets the fee. Adding Microsoft Advertising to a Google Ads account is a small increase; adding Meta with weekly creative testing is a larger one. It is agreed up front and revisited when scope changes.

**Can I get a quote without a call?** Yes. The form asks for monthly spend, platforms and what you are trying to fix, and a range comes back by email. A firm price needs a look at the account, which is a short call or read-only access.

**What if I only want a one-off fix, not management?** That is the audit, or a fixed-price project such as a setup or a tracking rebuild. Many engagements are exactly that and never become retainers.

Google Ads Search and monthly reporting · about eight months, 2019 to 2020 · reseller not named.

In October 2019, on almost the same spend as September (about R$ 9,300 a month), Google Ads produced 651 quote requests against 566. Cost per request fell from R$ 16.42 to R$ 14.31 and the conversion rate rose from 18.5% to 23.5%.

From the monthly report I prepared at the time, from Google Ads and Google Analytics. Two months side by side, not a trend. A quote request is a form submitted, not a plan sold. Full case on diwizi.com.

## Google Ads Management Services | Freelance, Flat Fee, Month to Month

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/google-ads-management/
Description: Google Ads management by an independent specialist with 14+ years: weekly work in the account, a written monthly report, flat fee, no long contract.

Ongoing management of Search, Shopping, Performance Max and YouTube campaigns, done by me every week, priced as a flat monthly fee and reported in the numbers an owner cares about.

## What Google Ads management services should actually include

Most management retainers are defined by what is excluded: tracking is a separate project, landing pages are your problem, reporting is a dashboard nobody reads. An account cannot perform under those conditions, so my definition of management is wider.

### Weekly, inside the account

Search terms read and negatives added. Bids, targets and budgets adjusted against cost per customer, not cost per click. Ads and assets rotated when a test has a clear winner. Auto-applied recommendations kept off and reviewed by a human.

### Measurement, maintained

Conversion actions checked monthly for double counting and breakage. GA4 and Tag Manager kept in step with site changes. Offline conversion import where sales close after the click. Included, not sold separately. See conversion tracking.

### Landing pages, in scope

Message match between ad and page, mobile speed, form and call tracking. Small changes I make myself; larger ones I specify for your developer. Paid traffic mostly dies on the page, so managing the account without the page is half a job.

### Reporting, in writing

A monthly document: cost per lead or per customer, revenue where it can be measured, what changed, what is next, and what I need from you. A call to go through it whenever you want one.

## Campaign types and how each one is handled

- Search. Structured by margin, service line and geography, because that is how you make decisions. Match types chosen deliberately, broad match only with the negatives and conversion data to support it. Brand kept in its own campaign so its numbers never flatter the rest.

- Performance Max. Brand exclusions from day one, asset groups split by product economics rather than by whatever the feed happened to contain, and a search-terms insight review every week to catch it buying demand you already had.

- Shopping. The feed is the campaign. Titles, GTINs, price competitiveness and custom labels come before bids. Standard Shopping kept where control over queries is worth more than reach. More on the ecommerce PPC page.

- YouTube and Demand Gen. Run for outcomes, not views: sequenced remarketing, offer-led creative, and conversion measurement that does not count a view as a lead.

- Microsoft Advertising. Imported and then actually managed, not left to sync. Often the cheapest incremental conversions in the account for B2B and finance. See Microsoft Advertising management.

## The first ninety days

- Weeks 1–2: measurement. Audit and fix every conversion action, reconcile Google Ads with GA4 and the CRM, define the one number the account will be optimised towards. Nothing else changes until this is right, because every later decision inherits it.

- Weeks 2–4: stop the leaks. Twelve months of search terms reviewed, negative lists built, brand and Performance Max exclusions set, budgets moved off the campaigns that produce cheap conversions with no margin.

- Weeks 4–8: structure. Rebuild or restructure where the current setup fights the business. Done in stages so learning is not reset across the whole account at once.

- Weeks 8–12: test. One control and one challenger at a time on ads, pages and offers, with enough volume to read the result. Report at day ninety on what moved, with the before and after in the same units.

## How the retainer is priced

A flat monthly fee, agreed after the audit and scaled by scope: number of campaigns, platforms, markets and how much landing page work is included. Not a percentage of spend, so the advice to cut budget costs me nothing to give. Month to month, with 30 days' notice either way. Ad spend is paid by you, directly to Google, from your own billing. The pricing page compares the models and gives typical ranges.

The account, the conversion actions, the tags and the landing pages stay in your properties. If the engagement ends, nothing needs to be rebuilt.

## Proof

Trutek, a truck parts company whose Google Ads I have run since 2020: about 260 attributed contact conversions from 5,707 clicks in the account's history. A health plan reseller: 651 quote requests in October 2019 at R$ 14.31 each. What was done and what each number does not prove is on the results page.

### FAQ

**How much do Google Ads management services cost?** A flat monthly fee set by scope, not by ad spend, quoted after a fixed-price audit that is credited against the first month. Send your monthly spend and platforms and you get a range back by email; the pricing page explains the model.

**How is a freelance Google Ads manager different from a management company?** The person you speak to is the person in the account, every week. A management company assigns the account to whoever has capacity and puts an account manager between you. The freelance model trades scale for continuity and seniority.

**Do you need a minimum ad spend?** No fixed minimum, but below roughly $3,000 a month a retainer is usually poor value; a one-off setup or audit fits better.

**How long until results show?** Tracking and wasted-spend fixes show within the first month. Structural and testing gains take a quarter to read properly, because bidding algorithms need conversion volume to settle. Anyone promising a number in week two is guessing.

**Will you manage the account in my Google Ads or yours?** Yours, always, via manager (MCC) access. Billing stays with you and nothing is built in an account I control.

**Can you manage Meta or Microsoft alongside Google?** Yes. Same person, same measurement layer, one report. See PPC management for the multi-platform version.

## PPC Management Services | Independent, Multi-Platform, Flat Fee

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/ppc-management/
Description: PPC management across Google, Microsoft and Meta Ads by one senior operator: one measurement layer, one report, one flat monthly fee.

Paid search and paid social run together: Google Ads and Microsoft Advertising for the demand that exists, Meta for the demand that has to be created, with one measurement layer deciding where the next dollar goes.

## Why multi-platform PPC management belongs with one person

When Google is run by one vendor and Meta by another, each one optimises its own dashboard and both claim the same conversions. Budget allocation becomes a negotiation between invoices rather than a decision based on incremental cost per customer. Putting the platforms under one operator with one tracking setup fixes the incentive before it fixes anything else.

It also means the platform mix follows the business. A B2B services company usually needs Google and Microsoft and very little Meta. A DTC brand needs Meta, Google Shopping and Performance Max and little else. A PPC management company that sells packages will sell you all of them; a single operator has no package to protect.

## Platforms and what each is for

| Platform | Used for | Typical share of budget |

| Google Ads | Capturing existing demand: Search, Shopping, Performance Max; remarketing on YouTube and Display | 50–80% |

| Microsoft Advertising | The same intent at a lower CPC, especially B2B, finance, older and desktop-heavy audiences | 5–15% |

| Meta Ads | Creating demand, remarketing, lead generation with instant forms where the product is simple | 10–40% |

Shares are starting points, moved monthly by measured cost per customer, not by platform reps.

## What the service includes

- One conversion definition across all platforms, deduplicated in GA4 and, where possible, tied to CRM stages so a Meta lead and a Google lead are compared on what they became, not on what the platform reports. See conversion tracking.

- Weekly management in every account: search terms and negatives, audiences and exclusions, creative rotation, bids and budgets.

- Cross-platform budget review each month, with a written recommendation on where to move spend and why.

- Landing pages and offers treated as part of the account, because the same page rarely works for a Google search click and a Meta feed click.

- One report, in your currency, on cost per customer by platform and in total.

## Who this is for, and who it is not for

It fits companies spending roughly $5,000 to $80,000 a month across two or more platforms who want a senior person accountable for the total rather than a vendor per channel. It fits agencies that need a senior operator on a client account without hiring; see white label PPC.

It does not fit brands that need creative production at volume as the main deliverable: for Meta-heavy DTC accounts I run the media and testing framework and work with your designer or a studio on the creative pipeline. And it does not fit companies looking for the cheapest PPC management services; the fee is set by seniority and scope, not by undercutting a marketplace listing.

## Pricing

A flat monthly retainer scaled by the number of platforms, markets and campaigns, agreed after a fixed-price audit of the accounts in scope. Not a percentage of spend. Month to month. Ad spend is paid by you to each platform directly. Details on the pricing page.

### FAQ

**What is the difference between PPC management and Google Ads management?** Google Ads management covers one platform. PPC management is the multi-platform version: Google plus Microsoft and Meta as needed, under one measurement layer and one report. Same person either way.

**Do you recommend adding platforms just to spend more?** No. Each platform is added when there is a measured reason, usually when the incremental cost per customer on the current platform is rising faster than the expected cost on the new one. The flat fee means I earn nothing from a bigger media plan.

**How do you compare a Meta lead with a Google lead fairly?** By what it becomes. Leads are pushed into your CRM with the source attached, and the comparison is made on qualified opportunities or revenue, not on the platforms' own conversion counts, which overlap and flatter themselves.

**Can you take over accounts from different vendors at once?** Yes. The audit covers all of them, tracking is unified first, and management starts once the numbers can be trusted. Transitions are staged so nothing loses learning at the same time.

**Is there a minimum spend for multi-platform management?** Around $5,000 a month in total is where two platforms start to make sense; below that, one platform run well beats two run thinly.

## Google Ads Setup Service | Account & Campaign Setup, Fixed Price

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/google-ads-setup/
Description: Fixed-price Google Ads setup by a 14-year specialist: structure, conversion tracking, negatives and landing page checks, built in your own account.

A fixed-price build for companies starting Google Ads, restarting after a bad experience, or launching a new market or product. Delivered inside your own account with tracking that works from day one, then handed over or kept under management, your choice.

## What goes wrong when Google Ads is set up quickly

Google makes it easy to launch a campaign in ten minutes, and the defaults it chooses are the ones that are good for Google: broad match, Smart Bidding with no data, Display and Search Partners switched on, auto-applied recommendations enabled, a conversion action that fires on a pageview. Most of the accounts I audit are still paying for a setup like that months later. A proper Google Ads campaign setup is slower and cheaper.

## What the setup includes

- Account foundations. Account created or cleaned in your name, billing on your card, manager access for me, GA4 and Tag Manager linked, auto-apply switched off, conversion actions defined for what you actually sell.

- Conversion tracking. Forms, calls, purchases or bookings tracked once each, deduplicated, tested on desktop and mobile, with enhanced conversions and consent mode where relevant. See conversion tracking setup for the full scope.

- Research and structure. Keyword research against your services and margins, competitor auction review, campaign structure by service line and geography, match types chosen on purpose, negative lists built before launch rather than after the first wasted month.

- Ads and assets. Responsive search ads written per ad group with real differentiation, sitelinks, callouts, structured snippets, call and location assets, brand campaign separated.

- Landing page check. Message match, speed, mobile forms and click-to-call tested. Fixes made where I can, specified for your developer where I cannot.

- Launch and first two weeks. Conservative bidding until data exists, daily checks during launch week, a written handover document explaining what was built and how to run it.

## Setup only, or setup then management

Many companies buy the setup and run it themselves, especially under $3,000 a month in spend, where a retainer would be a large share of the budget. The handover document is written for that: what each campaign is for, what to check weekly, what not to touch. Others move straight into month-to-month management. Starting management has no onboarding fee. Existing accounts start with an audit and new accounts with a setup; either one is a fixed price and is credited against the first month of management.

Either way, the build lives in your Google Ads account, and the tags in your Tag Manager. There is nothing to migrate later.

## Relaunches and new markets

A restart after an agency, a launch in Canada or the UK, or a new product line is a setup with history attached. In those cases the work begins with a short audit of what exists, so the good parts and the conversion data are kept and only the broken parts are rebuilt. Resetting an account to zero is rarely the right answer and always the easy one to sell.

### FAQ

**How much does a Google Ads setup cost?** A fixed price quoted from the form, scaled by the number of services, markets and whether tracking has to be built from scratch. Starting management has no onboarding fee. Existing accounts start with an audit and new accounts with a setup; either one is a fixed price and is credited against the first month of management.

**How long does it take?** Two to three weeks from kickoff to live for a typical single-market account. Tracking that depends on your developer or CRM can extend that.

**Do you set up the account in your MCC or mine?** Yours. If you do not have one, I create it in your name with your billing, then link it to my manager account for access. You can remove that access at any time.

**Can I run it myself afterwards?** Yes, and the handover document is written for that. A quarterly check-in or a one-off consulting session is available if you want a second pair of eyes without a retainer.

**Do you also set up Microsoft Advertising or Meta at the same time?** Yes. Microsoft is usually a small addition once Google is built. Meta is a separate build with its own tracking (pixel and Conversions API) and is quoted on its own.

## Facebook Ads Management | Meta & Instagram by a Freelance Specialist

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/meta-ads-management/
Description: Facebook and Instagram ads run by an independent specialist: Conversions API, structured creative tests and lead quality measured in your CRM. Flat fee.

Facebook and Instagram campaigns for lead generation and e-commerce, with tracking that survives iOS and ad blockers, a creative testing programme that produces winners on a schedule, and results judged on what the leads became.

## What a Meta Ads freelancer does differently from a Google Ads one

Google captures demand that already exists; Meta has to create it. That changes the whole job. On Meta, the creative is the targeting, the algorithm needs volume and consistency to learn, and the biggest lever is usually the offer rather than the audience settings. A Facebook ads consultant who treats it like search will spend a lot of your money on interest stacks that Meta stopped rewarding years ago.

### Measurement that holds up

Pixel plus Conversions API, event deduplication, and lead events matched back to CRM stages so a cheap lead that never answers the phone is not counted as a win. See conversion tracking.

### Structured creative testing

A fixed cadence of new concepts, each tested against the control with enough budget to read, winners scaled and losers retired. I run the framework and the media; creative production comes from your designer or a studio I work with.

### Simple structures

Broad or Advantage+ audiences with consolidated campaigns where the account has volume; tighter structures only where there is a measured reason. Fewer ad sets, more spend per learning phase.

## Lead generation and e-commerce, handled differently

### Lead generation

Instant forms produce cheap leads and a sales team that stops trusting them. The fix is usually a combination: higher-intent form questions, conditional logic, a landing page variant for comparison, and offline conversion upload of qualified and closed stages so Meta optimises towards the leads that turn into revenue. For home services, healthcare and B2B this matters more than any targeting change.

### E-commerce

Catalogue quality, Advantage+ Shopping alongside a controlled prospecting campaign, remarketing that is capped rather than left to run, and a clear view of new-customer cost separated from returning-customer revenue. Meta's reported ROAS and the store's actual margin are reconciled monthly, because they diverge.

## How Meta fits next to Google

Run together by one person, the two platforms stop competing for credit. Google Search picks up the demand Meta created; Meta remarketing closes the searchers who did not convert; and budget moves between them based on incremental cost per customer, not on which dashboard looks better. This is the core argument for multi-platform PPC management under one operator, and Meta is where it pays off most because Meta's self-reported numbers are the most generous.

## Audit, setup or ongoing

A Meta Ads audit can be bought on its own, and is included in the account audit when both platforms are in scope: tracking, structure, creative fatigue, frequency, audience overlap and the gap between reported and real results. Ongoing management is a flat monthly fee, month to month, with creative production billed by whoever makes it. Pricing follows the same model as everything else here; see pricing.

### FAQ

**How much does a freelance Facebook ads specialist cost?** A flat monthly fee for management, set by scope, plus whatever your creative production costs. Not a percentage of spend. A one-off audit is a fixed price. The pricing page has typical ranges.

**Do you produce the creative?** I write the copy, brief the concepts and run the testing framework. Image and video production comes from your designer or a studio, because a single operator cannot produce creative at the volume Meta rewards, and pretending otherwise is how accounts stall.

**Is Meta right for my business?** If the product can be understood from a feed post and the margin supports a cost per lead that includes some unqualified ones, usually yes. For high-ticket B2B with long cycles, Google typically comes first and Meta serves as remarketing. I will say which on the call.

**How do you deal with iOS tracking loss?** Conversions API alongside the pixel, deduplicated events, enhanced matching, and offline conversion uploads from the CRM. Reported numbers are still modelled; the CRM is the source of truth for decisions.

**Can you audit an existing Meta account before I commit?** Yes. The audit is fixed price, does not require moving anything, and is credited against the first month if you continue.

## Microsoft Ads Management | Bing Ads Run by a Freelance Specialist

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/microsoft-ads-management/
Description: Microsoft Ads (Bing Ads) management: imported from Google, then actually run with its own negatives, bids and reporting. Flat monthly fee.

Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo, Copilot and the Microsoft network reach a desktop-heavy, older and more B2B audience at a lower cost per click than Google for the same query. Most accounts import the Google campaigns once and never open the platform again.

## Why Microsoft Advertising is worth managing rather than syncing

The import tool makes it easy to mirror Google Ads into Microsoft Advertising, and the sync keeps the two aligned. That is also the problem: the Microsoft audience is different, the auction is thinner, and the query mix skews towards desktop, older users, corporate networks where Edge and Bing are the default, and now Copilot. A campaign that is right for Google is usually over-bid, under-negatived and mis-scheduled on Microsoft.

- B2B and professional services see the biggest gap, because corporate desktops default to Edge and Bing far more than consumer phones do.

- Finance, insurance, legal and healthcare reach an older audience that converts well and costs less per click.

- Local services benefit from lower competition: many local advertisers never set Microsoft up at all.

## What management includes

- Import, then diverge. Google campaigns imported as a starting point, sync limited to what should stay aligned (ads, sitelinks), and bids, budgets, schedules and negatives managed natively.

- Conversion tracking. UET tag through Tag Manager, goals mapped to the same definitions as Google, enhanced conversions and offline import where sales close later. One measurement layer for both engines.

- Microsoft-specific settings. Search partner network reviewed and usually restricted, LinkedIn profile targeting used where it fits (company, industry, job function are available here and not on Google), device and location adjustments set for a desktop-heavy audience.

- Weekly search terms. Microsoft's query matching is looser than Google's, so the negative list needs its own maintenance rather than a copy.

- Reporting alongside Google. Same units, same report, so incremental cost per customer on Microsoft is visible and budget can move accordingly.

## How much budget belongs on Microsoft

Typically 5% to 15% of the paid search budget in the US and UK, higher for B2B. The right number is found by measuring, not assumed: Microsoft campaigns start with a modest budget, conversion volume is watched for a month, and spend follows cost per customer. The point is not that Microsoft replaces Google; it is that, in the accounts I have run, the same conversion has often cost noticeably less there, and leaving it unmanaged leaves that on the table.

## Setup, audit or ongoing

Microsoft Advertising is usually added to a Google Ads management retainer as a modest scope increase, or built as part of a setup project. An existing Microsoft account can be included in the audit. Pricing follows the flat-fee model on the pricing page.

### FAQ

**Is Bing Ads worth it in 2026?** For most B2B, finance, legal, healthcare and local service accounts in the US and UK, yes: the same conversions at a lower cost per click, with less competition. For very young or mobile-first consumer audiences, less so. The test costs little and the answer is usually clear within a month.

**Can I just import my Google campaigns and leave it?** You can, and most people do, which is why the accounts I inherit are over-bidding on desktop and running the search partner network unfiltered. Import is the start, not the management.

**What does Microsoft Advertising management cost?** Added to a Google Ads retainer it is a small increase in the flat fee. As a standalone account it is priced by scope like anything else, and rarely justifies its own retainer below a few thousand in monthly spend.

**Do you manage Microsoft on its own, without Google?** Rarely, because the Google account is usually where the structure and data come from. If Google is run by someone else, I can still manage Microsoft separately, but it works better under one operator; see PPC management.

## Ecommerce PPC Management | Google Shopping & Performance Max

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/ecommerce-ppc-management/
Description: Ecommerce PPC by an independent consultant: Shopping feeds, Performance Max with brand exclusions and Meta for new customers, judged on margin, not ROAS.

Google Shopping, Performance Max, Search and Meta for online stores, run by one person who separates the revenue you would have had anyway from the revenue the ads produced.

## What an ecommerce PPC consultant should be looking at

Platform ROAS is the most flattering number in paid media. Performance Max claims your brand searches, Meta claims your returning customers, and both report a return that would make any store profitable. Ecommerce PPC management that is worth paying for starts by separating three things: revenue from new customers, revenue from existing ones, and revenue that would have arrived without ads. Budget decisions are made on the first, with margin rather than revenue as the unit.

### The feed is the campaign

Titles rewritten for how people search, GTINs and attributes completed, price competitiveness checked against the Merchant Center report, custom labels for margin, seasonality and stock so campaigns can be split on what matters.

### Performance Max, contained

Brand terms excluded, asset groups built around product economics, search term insights reviewed weekly, a Standard Shopping campaign kept where query control beats reach.

### Meta for new customers

Advantage+ Shopping with a new-customer cap where it works, prospecting on creative rather than interests, remarketing frequency capped, and results reconciled against store data rather than Meta's own attribution. See Meta Ads.

## What management includes

- Measurement. Purchase tracking with enhanced conversions and Conversions API, revenue and item data correct, new versus returning customer flagged, and a monthly reconciliation between platform-reported revenue and the store's order data. See conversion tracking.

- Feed and Merchant Center. Disapprovals cleared, feed rules and supplemental feeds maintained, promotions and shipping set up, price benchmarks reviewed.

- Campaign structure by economics. Products grouped by margin and price tier, not by category tree; brand, non-brand and competitor search separated; PMax and Shopping given distinct roles.

- Weekly optimisation. Search terms and negatives, target ROAS or CPA moved with margin and stock, budgets shifted between platforms on incremental new-customer cost.

- Seasonal planning. Budgets, bids and creative staged ahead of peaks, and a plan for the quiet weeks that does not involve buying your own brand.

## Who this fits

Stores spending roughly $5,000 to $80,000 a month across Google and Meta, on Shopify, WooCommerce, BigCommerce or a custom stack, with a margin structure that can be shared so campaigns can be run against it. It fits less well for marketplaces-only sellers and for stores whose main need is creative production at volume, where I run the media and testing framework alongside a studio rather than replacing it.

## Audit first

Ecommerce accounts benefit more than most from a fixed-price audit before anything changes: the gap between reported and incremental revenue is usually the biggest finding, and it changes what the account should be doing. Management is a flat monthly fee, month to month; see pricing.

### FAQ

**What does ecommerce PPC management cost?** A flat monthly fee set by scope: platforms, catalogue size, markets. Not a percentage of spend or of revenue. Audit first, credited against the first month. See pricing.

**Should I run Performance Max or Standard Shopping?** Usually both, with different jobs: PMax for reach across Google's inventory with brand excluded, Standard Shopping where you need control over queries and products. The split depends on the catalogue and the data, and it is one of the first things the audit settles.

**What ROAS should I expect?** The honest answer is that platform ROAS is not the target; contribution margin after ad spend on new customers is. A store with 60% gross margin and a 3x ROAS is in a very different position from one with 25% margin and the same ROAS. I will build the target from your numbers, not from a benchmark.

**Do you manage Amazon Ads?** No. Google, Microsoft and Meta for the store's own site. For Amazon I can recommend specialists.

**Do you work with our developer on the feed?** Yes. Most feed work can be done through Merchant Center rules and supplemental feeds without touching the store; where a platform change is needed, I specify it for your developer.

## Google Ads for Small Business | PPC Management Sized to the Budget

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/small-business-ppc-management/
Description: Google Ads for small business: what the budget buys, when it is not worth it, and a fixed-price setup you run yourself, an audit or a lean flat-fee retainer.

For local and small companies spending a few thousand a month, the usual choice is a marketplace freelancer at one end and an agency with a minimum retainer at the other. There is a middle: a senior specialist, a lean scope and a fee that makes sense for the spend.

## Why small business Google Ads accounts underperform

The mechanics are the same as in a $50,000 account, but the margin for error is smaller. A duplicated conversion action, a broad-match campaign with no negatives or a service area set to the whole metro will waste a third of a small budget before anyone notices. And the market for helping small businesses is full of two bad options: very cheap management that is really an import-and-forget, and agency retainers whose minimum fee is bigger than the media budget.

## What a small business budget actually buys

The arithmetic is simpler than the pitch decks make it. Budget divided by cost per click gives clicks; clicks times the conversion rate of the landing page gives inquiries; inquiries times your close rate gives customers. Cost per click depends on the sector: legal, finance and insurance pay the most per click, local trades and professional services sit in the middle, retail and food at the bottom. The table uses round numbers to show the shape, not a forecast for your account.

| Monthly budget | At $5 a click | At $20 a click | At $60 a click |

| $1,000 | 200 clicks, about 20 inquiries | 50 clicks, about 5 inquiries | 16 clicks, 1 or 2 inquiries |

| $3,000 | 600 clicks, about 60 inquiries | 150 clicks, about 15 inquiries | 50 clicks, about 5 inquiries |

| $10,000 | 2,000 clicks, about 200 inquiries | 500 clicks, about 50 inquiries | 166 clicks, about 16 inquiries |

Inquiries assume one visitor in ten acts, which is what a focused landing page on a phone can do for a local service and what a homepage rarely does. Two things follow. At the expensive end, $1,000 a month buys a handful of inquiries, so one wasted click in three is the difference between profit and loss; that is where setup quality matters most. At the cheap end, the constraint is not budget but whether you can answer every call and quote fast, because the account will produce more inquiries than a two-person business expects.

## When Google Ads is not worth it for a small business

- Nobody searches for it. Google Ads captures demand; it does not create it. A new category, or a product people do not know they need, belongs on Meta first, or in a referral program.

- The margin cannot carry the click. If a sale earns you $40 and a click costs $8, you need one sale in five clicks to break even. Few landing pages do that. Raise the price, sell a bundle, or sell a service around the product.

- Nobody can pick up the phone. Most local inquiries call. If calls go to voicemail between 9 and 5, the budget pays for other people's customers.

- The website does not work on a phone. Fixing that comes first; a page is cheaper than a month of wasted clicks. See landing pages.

- Less than about $1,000 a month in a competitive category. Below that, the account cannot gather enough data to learn, and the fixed cost of doing it properly outweighs the result. A one-off setup you run yourself is the honest option.

I say so on the first call when any of these applies. The fee is flat, so there is no incentive to recommend spend that will not pay.

## Do it yourself, or hire someone

Google's own onboarding pushes small advertisers toward Smart campaigns, Performance Max and auto-applied recommendations. They are designed to spend the budget with little input, which is not the same as spending it well: broad targeting, no search terms to read, and no way to tell a call from a misdial. A small business can run its own account, but on a Search campaign built properly, with exact and phrase match, a negative list, call tracking and conversion actions that count real inquiries.

- Do it yourself when spend is under $3,000 a month, one person can give it an hour a week, and the account was built by someone who knew what they were doing. That is the setup option: built, documented and handed over, with a quarterly check-in if you want one.

- Hire management when spend passes $3,000, when nobody has the hour a week, or when the account has been running for a year without anyone reading the search terms. At that point the fee is usually smaller than the waste it removes.

- Get an audit first when an agency or a previous freelancer ran the account and you cannot tell whether it worked. Fixed price, written findings, no obligation.

## Two ways to buy this, by budget

| Monthly ad spend | What makes sense | What it involves |

| Under $3,000 | Fixed-price setup, then run it yourself | Account built properly with tracking, negatives and a handover document. A quarterly check-in if you want one. |

| Over $3,000 | Standard management retainer | Weekly work, tracking and landing pages in scope, full monthly report. |

The fee is flat at every tier, never a percentage of spend, so the advice to keep the budget small is free to give.

## What local PPC management focuses on

- Service area that matches the trucks. Bidding across the whole metro when you cover half of it means paying for jobs you will decline. Radius, zip or city targeting set to where you actually go, with bid adjustments for the areas that pay best.

- Calls tracked as calls, and as jobs. Call tracking with the keyword behind the call, plus a simple way for you to mark which calls became jobs, so the account learns from revenue rather than ring volume.

- Emergency and planned work separated. An urgent repair and a quote request are different buyers, different bids and different pages. Merged, the urgent work subsidises the browsing.

- Local Services Ads alongside Search where the category qualifies, with the two measured together.

- A landing page that works on a phone, with a click-to-call button that is tracked. Most local paid traffic is mobile and most local landing pages are not.

## The proof, at small-business scale

The published cases are small and mid-sized accounts: a Brazilian truck parts company with about 260 attributed contact conversions since 2020, and a health plan reseller with 651 quote requests in one month at R$ 14.31 each. The tactics above are the ones I use, and they scale down. The results page has the detail and the limits. Industry-specific pages for HVAC, plumbing, cleaning, dental, legal and others are on diwizi.com.

### FAQ

**How much does small business PPC management cost?** Depends on the tier above. A setup is a one-off fixed price; management is a flat monthly fee; both are quoted by email from the form. Never a percentage of spend. See pricing.

**Is Google Ads worth it for a small budget?** For a local service with a clear search demand, usually yes even at $1,000 to $2,000 a month, provided the account is set up properly and the landing page converts on mobile. For products with low margin or no search demand, often no, and I will say so.

**Can I run the account myself after setup?** Yes. The handover document is written for an owner, and a quarterly consulting session is available for a second look without a retainer.

**Do you handle Local Services Ads?** Yes, where the category qualifies, and measured together with Search so budget goes to whichever produces the cheaper booked job.

**Do you work with businesses outside the US?** Yes: Canada, Europe, and any country where the business works in English. Local targeting and call tracking work the same way; the currency in the report changes.

**How much should a small business spend on Google Ads?** Enough to buy at least 100 clicks a month in your category, because below that the account cannot learn which keywords and ads work. At $10 a click that is $1,000; at $50 a click, $5,000. Start there for two months, read the cost per inquiry, and scale what pays. Spending less in a competitive category is usually worse than not advertising.

**Should a small business use Performance Max or Smart campaigns?** Not as the first campaign. Both hide the search terms and decide for you where the budget goes, which suits Google more than a $2,000 a month account. Start with a Search campaign you can read; add Performance Max later, with brand excluded, once conversion tracking is reliable and there is data for it to learn from.

**How long before a small Google Ads account shows results?** The first inquiries usually arrive in the first week if the setup is right; a reliable cost per inquiry takes six to eight weeks, because a small budget produces a small sample. Decisions in the first month are about waste (search terms, locations, hours), not about scaling.

## When an agency needs white label PPC

What is not covered: account management in the client-facing sense. I do not run your client relationship, chase approvals or attend your weekly status call unless you ask me to join as your specialist.

## Pricing for agencies

Per account, flat monthly, scaled by scope, with a lower unit price as the number of accounts grows. Not a percentage of the client's spend and not a share of your retainer. Audits for pitches are a fixed price each. Capacity is limited on purpose, so I take on a small number of agency partners rather than a queue; the pricing page explains the model and the contact page is the way to start.

### FAQ

**How is white label PPC priced?** A flat monthly fee per account, set by scope, with volume pricing for several accounts. Not a percentage of the client's spend, so you can price your retainer however you like.

**Can you audit a prospect's account for a pitch?** Yes, as a fixed-price deliverable in your template. It is the same audit I sell directly, with your name on it.

**What if you are at capacity?** I say so before taking the account. Over-committing is how white label work gets a bad reputation, and I would rather refer you on than run your client's account badly.

**Do you sign an NDA and a non-solicit?** Yes to both, as standard. Your clients are yours.

## GA4 & Google Tag Manager Consultant | Conversion Tracking Setup

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/conversion-tracking-setup/
Description: Conversion tracking set up or repaired for Google Ads, Microsoft and Meta: GA4, Tag Manager, enhanced conversions, consent mode and CRM import. Fixed price.

If the conversion data is wrong, every bidding decision inherits the error. This is a fixed-price project to make Google Ads, GA4, Meta and your CRM agree on what a customer is, and to keep them agreeing.

## What broken tracking looks like from inside the account

- Three conversion actions for one lead: form submit, thank-you pageview and a phone call, all set to count every conversion. Reported cost per lead is a third of the truth.

- Google Ads says 80 conversions, GA4 says 55, the CRM has 31 leads and the sales team says 9 were real. Nobody can say which number to optimise towards, so Smart Bidding optimises towards 80.

- Tags fire before consent, or not at all after the cookie banner update. Half the conversions disappeared in March and were blamed on the market.

- Meta and Google each claim the same purchase. Combined reported revenue is 140% of what the store took.

- Sales close six weeks after the click, in the CRM, and the ad platforms never hear about it. They keep buying the leads that fill forms fastest, which are the worst ones.

## What the setup includes

- Definitions first. A short document naming each outcome that matters (qualified lead, booked call, purchase, opportunity, closed deal), its value, and which platform counts it as primary. This is agreed with you before a single tag changes.

- Google Tag Manager as the single layer. Google Ads, GA4, Meta and any other platform tags (LinkedIn included) managed in one container, with a data layer for forms, calls and purchases, versioned and documented.

- Google Ads conversions rebuilt. One action per outcome, correct counting (one vs every), attribution and value settings, enhanced conversions for leads and for web, call tracking with keyword-level data, and old actions retired properly so history is not lost.

- GA4 aligned. Key events matching the definitions, cross-domain where needed, internal traffic excluded, and GA4 imports to Google Ads used only where they should be.

- Consent mode configured to your banner and region, so measurement survives the law and the modelling has something to model.

- Meta server-side. Conversions API alongside the pixel, event deduplication, enhanced matching.

- Offline conversion import. Qualified, opportunity and closed stages pushed back from HubSpot, Salesforce or a sheet to Google and Meta, so the platforms learn from revenue. This is the step that changes accounts the most and is skipped the most.

- Testing and handover. Every event tested on desktop and mobile, a reconciliation report showing the platforms and the CRM agreeing, and a document explaining what fires where and how to check it.

## Why this is a separate project and also part of every retainer

Tracking is the first thing fixed in any management engagement and the first section of every audit, and it is maintained monthly for ongoing clients because sites change and tags break. It is also sold on its own, because many companies have a capable in-house or agency team running the campaigns and simply cannot trust the numbers. A tracking rebuild without a retainer attached is a common and sensible purchase.

## Pricing and time

Fixed price, quoted after the form and a look at the current setup, scaled by the number of platforms, outcomes and whether CRM integration is in scope. Typically one to three weeks, with the CRM piece depending on access. Included in management retainers; credited against the first month if a retainer follows. See pricing.

### FAQ

**How much does conversion tracking setup cost?** A fixed price scaled by platforms and outcomes. A Google Ads and GA4 rebuild for a lead generation site is at the low end; adding Meta server-side and CRM offline import is at the high end. Quoted after a look at what exists.

**Do you need access to our website code?** Usually Google Tag Manager access is enough. A data layer push from forms or the checkout sometimes needs a developer; I specify it exactly and test it once it is in place.

**Can you fix tracking without managing the ads?** Yes. It is a standalone project, and often the most valuable thing an in-house or agency-run account can buy.

**What is offline conversion import and do we need it?** Sending later outcomes, such as a qualified lead or a closed deal from your CRM, back to the ad platforms with the original click ID, so they optimise towards revenue instead of form fills. If sales close after the click, you need it; it is the single biggest lever in lead generation accounts.

**Will this handle GDPR and consent?** Consent mode is configured to your banner and regions so tags respect consent and Google can model what it cannot observe. I set up the technical side; the legal choice of banner behaviour is yours or your counsel's.
