## B2B PPC Consultant | Google Ads Measured in Pipeline, Not Leads

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/b2b-ppc/
Description: B2B PPC by an independent consultant: Google and Microsoft Search for buyers already looking, CRM-connected and reported in pipeline. Flat fee.

B2B accounts fail in a specific way: the platforms are optimizing toward form fills, the sales team is ignoring them, and nobody can say which campaign produced the last closed deal. Connecting the CRM to the ad platforms is most of the job, and it is where a B2B engagement starts here.

## Where B2B accounts leak

- Leads counted, pipeline not. A whitepaper download and a demo request from a named account are both "a lead" to the platform. Until MQL, SQL and opportunity stages flow back from HubSpot or Salesforce, the platforms buy the cheapest form fill, which is the least qualified one.

- Brand taking the credit. Broad match and Performance Max drift onto the company name and the reported cost per lead looks excellent. Brand is isolated, and the non-brand number is the one managed.

- Research and job-seeker traffic. "What is", "salary", "jobs", "free template": expensive clicks from people who will never buy. Twelve months of search terms read line by line, then a negatives program maintained weekly.

- One page for every intent. A category search, a competitor comparison and an integration search deserve different pages with different asks.

## What management includes

- Measurement to the CRM. GA4 and Tag Manager with campaign data attached to every lead, HubSpot, Salesforce or Pipedrive stages imported to Google Ads and Microsoft Advertising as offline conversions with amounts, enhanced conversions for leads. See conversion tracking.

- Google Search by intent. Category, problem, integration and competitor campaigns, each with its own page and target, brand kept separate, Performance Max only with brand excluded and only once the conversion data deserves it.

- Microsoft Advertising for the professional audience on work devices, with LinkedIn profile bid adjustments Google cannot offer. Microsoft Ads →

- Pages per intent, built by me: comparison pages, integration pages, use-case pages, with a form that asks the one qualifying question. See landing pages.

- Reporting in pipeline. Qualified pipeline, closed-won revenue and cost per opportunity by channel and segment, alongside the platform numbers, in your currency.

## Published B2B results

Two of the cases on results sell to businesses: Trutek, whose Google Ads account shows about 260 attributed contact conversions since 2020, and Pontomais, a B2B software company where I rebuilt the Google Ads account as an employee and contact requests went from about five in a month to the hundreds in eight months. Each figure is labeled with its source and its limits. The method was the one above.

## Who this fits

US and Canadian B2B companies, and companies from any country that work in English: SaaS, professional and technical services, industrial suppliers, consultancies, spending roughly $5,000 to $80,000 a month on Google and Microsoft, with a CRM in use. LinkedIn Ads can be added when a named-account campaign is worth the click price; it is not the core of the work. Below that, Google Search alone with the CRM connected is usually the right first step, and I will say so. For software companies specifically, see SaaS PPC.

### FAQ

**What is a good cost per lead for B2B PPC?** The wrong question, politely. Cost per qualified opportunity and cost per closed deal are the numbers, and they only exist once the CRM is connected. From that point the targets come from your deal size and sales cycle, not from an industry benchmark.

**Can you connect Google Ads to our CRM?** Yes: HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive and most others with an API or native integration. Offline conversion import with stage and amount, enhanced conversions for leads, and campaign data stored on every record so sales can see where a deal came from.

**Should we bid on competitor names?** Usually yes, in a separate campaign with its own comparison page and a target that reflects the lower conversion rate. Honest comparison pages convert well and stay within the advertising rules.

**How much does B2B PPC management cost?** A flat monthly fee set from the scope: platforms, markets, campaigns and how much landing page and tracking work is included. Never a percentage of spend. Quoted in US dollars, pounds or euros by email from the form. See pricing.

## PPC Landing Pages and Websites | Built by the Consultant Who Runs the Ads

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/landing-pages/
Description: Campaign landing pages and 3 to 8 page business websites built by the consultant who runs the ads. Copy, build, tracking, hosting and the paperwork, in one fixed scope.

Most paid accounts are optimized up to the click and abandoned after it. The ad agency does not own the website; the web agency does not read the ad account. Here the same person does both: campaign pages, and when the site itself cannot carry the campaign, a business website of 3 to 8 pages, built from the search terms, measured from the first visit and changed from the data. Hosting, tracking and the paperwork around a launch are in scope, so you approve copy, answer a short brief, and nothing else lands on your desk.

## Why the page is usually the problem

- The homepage as the landing page. Someone who searched for emergency AC repair lands on a page about the company's history, twelve services and a careers link. The page has to answer the search in the first screen.

- A form built for the company, not the visitor. Nine fields, a captcha, no phone number on mobile. Every field removed is measured in inquiries.

- No message match. The ad promises a fixed price; the page says "contact us for a quote". The visitor leaves and the click is paid for either way.

- Slow on a phone. Most paid clicks for services are on mobile; a page that takes six seconds on a cellular connection loses a third of them before it loads.

- Nothing is tested. One page since launch, no record of what was tried. Conversion rate optimization is a program, not a redesign.

## What the work includes

- One page per intent, from the account. The search terms, the ads and the call recordings decide what each page says. Services get one page each; B2B gets comparison, integration and use-case pages.

- Built by me, in plain HTML. Hand coded static pages hosted on your domain or on a subdomain you control, no WordPress, no page builder, no plugin to break. No agency queue, no three-week change request.

- A business website when the site is the problem. Three to five pages for a basic site or five to eight for a Performance site: home, services, about, proof and contact, plus the pages a buyer reads before calling. Built for the campaigns rather than for a design portfolio, as hand coded HTML pages that load fast and have no CMS to maintain. Online stores and brand identity work are not included, and I will say so.

- Tracked before it goes live. GA4, Tag Manager, Google Ads enhanced conversions, the Meta Conversions API, call tracking and the form connected and tested, so the first visit is measured. See conversion tracking.

- Fast and compliant. Core Web Vitals checked on a real mobile connection, consent handled, accessibility basics in place.

- A test program. One change at a time, with enough traffic to read the result, recorded so the next person knows what was tried. Headline, offer, form length, proof, phone placement, in that order of likely impact.

## Hosting, maintenance and the paperwork

A page needs a dozen small things around it before it earns a dollar. They are part of the job, not a list you get handed at the end.

- Domain, DNS and SSL. Registered or transferred in your name, pointed and secured.

- Hosting under your domain. Static pages on infrastructure I manage, with backups, or your existing host if you have one. Hosting is part of the monthly maintenance, basic or full, not a separate bill.

- Consent and privacy. Cookie banner with Consent Mode where your visitors require it, privacy page text, and forms with spam protection that reach your inbox and your CRM.

- Accounts connected. Google Search Console, Google Business Profile, GA4, Tag Manager and the ad accounts verified and linked.

- Maintenance. Basic: hosting, SSL, backups and a warning if the site goes down. Full: also updates, a monthly check that every tag still fires and one hour of changes a month. Billed month to month.

- Handover and invoices. Every login documented, code and content yours, and invoices your bookkeeper can file without a question.

## Plans, priced on request

Standalone projects come at two levels: Simple, a template in your brand with the essential tracking, and Performance, designed for you, with full tracking and two revision rounds. Each is quoted on request, in US dollars for the United States and Canada, pounds for the UK and euros for the rest of Europe, with the scope in writing before any work starts. Inside a management retainer, building and testing pages is part of running the account, not a change request. Either way the pages, the code and the accounts belong to you and live on your domain.

- Meta Ads ready

## What a landing page changes

In the accounts I run, part of the result is the account and part is the pages: one per service instead of one for the company, the phone number and the booking form in the first screen, and the promise in the ad repeated on the page.

### FAQ

**Do you design the pages or just the copy?** Both, within a system: your brand's fonts and colors, a layout built for the intent, copy from the search terms and the sales calls. For heavy custom design a designer on your side or a studio produces the visuals and I build and test the page.

**Which platforms can you build on?** Plain HTML, hosted on your domain or on a subdomain you control, with or without hosting by me. I do not build in WordPress or page builders. If the page has to live inside your CMS, I deliver the HTML and your developer embeds it.

**Do you build full websites?** Yes, when the site cannot carry the campaign: a basic website of three to five pages or a Performance website of five to eight, copy included, built for the campaigns and tracked from day one, with hosting in the monthly maintenance. Not online stores and not brand identity work; for those I will point you to someone better.

**How much does a landing page or a website cost?** Included in management retainers: for clients whose campaigns I run, a new page or an A/B test is part of the retainer, not a separate fee. As a standalone project, each landing page, website, tracking setup or maintenance plan is quoted on request, in US dollars, pounds or euros, with the scope in writing before any work starts. Half on approval, half on delivery. The plans above show what each one includes.

**Do you host the pages?** Optional, and quoted both ways. Without hosting you get the HTML files installed on your host. With hosting, the page lives under your domain on infrastructure I manage: a basic plan with SSL and backups, or a full plan that adds updates, a monthly check that every tag still fires and one hour of changes a month. The monthly amount is quoted with the page.

**How do I pay?** By bank transfer through Wise, invoiced in US dollars, pounds or euros, with half on approval of the written scope and half on delivery. I do not take card payments.

**Can my agency resell the pages?** Yes. The same page is available white label, with no mention of me, delivered under your agency's name. See white label PPC.

**Can you improve our existing pages instead of building new ones?** Yes. A conversion review of the current pages against the account data comes first, and often the fixes are to the form, the first screen and the speed rather than a rebuild.

**How long until a test shows a result?** It depends on traffic: a page with 1,000 paid visits a month can read a meaningful change in two to four weeks; a page with 100 cannot, and the program is adjusted to test bigger changes less often.

## YouTube Ads Management | Video Campaigns Measured in Leads and Sales

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/youtube-ads-management/
Description: YouTube Ads management by an independent Google Ads specialist: in-stream, Shorts and Demand Gen measured in leads and sales, not views.

YouTube is the cheapest reach in Google Ads and the easiest place to spend without result. Run as part of the Search account, with the same conversion tracking and the same person judging both, video can create the demand Search then captures. Run on its own and measured in views, it rarely pays.

## Why YouTube budgets disappear

- Measured in views and view rate. A view is counted at 30 seconds or a click; neither is a customer. The campaign is judged on conversions and on the lift in branded search and Search conversions during the flight.

- Audiences left to the default. Without custom segments built from your own search terms, competitor channels and in-market signals, the campaign reaches whoever is cheapest.

- One creative, run until it dies. Video wears out faster than text. A program of hooks and cuts, tested against each other, is the difference between a campaign that keeps working and one that spikes and fades.

- Demand Gen switched on as a bet. Demand Gen reaches YouTube, Discover and Gmail with the same creative and Google's audience modeling. It can work for considered purchases and lead generation; it needs conversion data to learn from and brand excluded from the credit.

## What management includes

- Objective and measurement first. Conversion actions shared with Search, view-through windows set deliberately and reported separately, brand search lift tracked during flights. See conversion tracking.

- Audience architecture. Custom segments from your search terms and competitors' names, in-market and life-event segments where they fit, remarketing from site visitors and the CRM, exclusions for existing customers.

- Format by job. Skippable in-stream for consideration, Shorts and bumpers for frequency, Demand Gen for lead generation and considered purchases, video action campaigns where the conversion data supports them.

- Creative program. Briefs for hooks in the first five seconds, cuts at 6, 15 and 30 seconds, vertical versions for Shorts, produced by your team or a studio, tested against a control and retired on a schedule.

- One report with Search. YouTube and Demand Gen next to Search, Shopping and Performance Max, with the conversions each produced and the effect on branded search, so the budget split follows the numbers.

## Who this fits

Companies already running Search with conversion tracking that works, and with a product or service that benefits from being explained or shown: SaaS, considered consumer purchases, education, healthcare, higher-value home services. Usually $3,000 a month or more on video alongside Search. Brands that want views and reach as the objective are better served by a media agency, and I will say so. YouTube is managed as part of Google Ads management rather than as a separate retainer.

### FAQ

**How much does YouTube advertising cost?** Cost per view is commonly a few cents; what matters is cost per lead or sale, which only exists once the campaign shares the Search account's conversion tracking. Management is part of a Google Ads retainer, a flat fee set from the scope. See pricing.

**Do you produce the video?** I write the briefs, the hooks and the cuts to test; your team or a studio produces the footage. Many successful campaigns run on edits of existing video, phone-shot founder pieces and product demos.

**Is Demand Gen worth it?** For lead generation and considered purchases with enough conversion data, often yes, with brand excluded so the reported result is real. For low-value transactions, usually not. It is tested against a budget and a target, not switched on as a bet.

**Can you run YouTube without Google Search?** Yes, but it is rarely the right order. Search captures the demand video creates, and without it the result of the video is hard to see and harder to keep.

## Google Ads Expert | Senior Google Ads Specialist, Hired Directly

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/google-ads-expert/
Description: Hire a Google Ads expert directly: a senior PPC specialist with 14+ years on the account, working with you instead of through an agency. Flat fee.

Expert and specialist are words every agency uses in its pitch. This page sets out what a senior Google Ads specialist actually does differently, how to check it before you hire one, and how the engagement works when the expert is the person you deal with.

## What a senior specialist does that a generalist or a junior does not

- Reads the search terms before touching the bids. Most waste in lead generation accounts is in what gets counted and in the queries matched, not in the bidding. A specialist starts there.

- Treats the automation as a tool with settings, not as a strategy. Smart Bidding and Performance Max are switched on when the conversion data deserves them and reviewed with brand excluded, so the reported result is real.

- Owns the measurement. GA4, Tag Manager, consent and the CRM are part of the job, because an expert cannot optimize toward a number that is wrong.

- Builds the page after the click. The landing page is usually the largest lever in the account and the one nobody who runs the ads has touched. Here it is included.

- Says no. To budget increases the data does not support, to platforms that do not fit the business, to accounts that need an agency rather than one person.

## How to check a Google Ads expert before hiring one

- Ask who will be in the account weekly. If the answer is a team, ask for the name and the years of experience of the person doing the work. Here the answer is one name, and it is the person you spoke to.

- Ask for a written review before any retainer. An expert can read your account read-only and tell you in writing what is wrong and what it costs each month. That is the Google Ads audit, and it stands on its own.

- Ask how results are reported. Platform numbers alone are a warning sign. The report should reconcile to your CRM or your orders, with brand and non-brand shown separately.

- Ask what they will not do. An expert has a scope. Mine is Google, Microsoft and Meta Ads for businesses spending roughly $3,000 to $80,000 a month, with the exceptions listed on the home page.

- Check the published work. Named cases where the client allowed it, anonymized where they did not, with the figures and their source stated. Results →

## Expert, consultant, freelancer: which word applies

People search for all three and the work is the same person. "Expert" and "specialist" describe depth on the platform; "consultant" describes advice and reviews available without a retainer; "freelancer" describes the independence from an agency. All three are true here, and none of them is the point. The point is that the senior person is the one in the account.

## How an engagement with an expert starts

Read-only access, a fixed-price written review, then your choice: implement it yourselves, hire me for the fixes, or have me run the account month to month with 30 days' notice either way. Fees are flat, set from the scope, never a percentage of spend, and quoted in US dollars, pounds or euros by email from the form.

### FAQ

**How much does a Google Ads expert cost?** Senior US freelancers commonly quote by the hour or a flat monthly retainer; agencies commonly charge a percentage of spend with a minimum. My fee is flat, set from the scope of the account, and quoted by email from the form. See pricing.

**What is the difference between a Google Ads expert and an agency?** Who does the work. An agency puts an account team between you and the account, usually led by someone junior once the pitch is over. An expert is the person doing the work, and you speak to them directly.

**Are you a Google Partner?** No. I am Google Ads certified, but not a Google Partner, which is a separate status with its own spend and performance requirements. Neither badge tells you who will work on your account. What you can check is the written review, the published cases and how the first call goes.

**Can you work alongside our in-house marketer?** Yes. A common arrangement is a monthly review of the work your team does, with a written note and a call, or a setup that your team then runs. The scope is agreed in writing at the start.

**Which platforms are you an expert in?** Google Ads first, including Shopping, Performance Max, YouTube and Demand Gen; then Microsoft Advertising and Meta Ads, with GA4, Tag Manager and landing pages as part of every engagement.

## PPC for Law Firms | Google Ads for Attorneys, Run by One Consultant

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/ppc-for-law-firms/
Description: PPC for law firms: Google Ads by practice area, intake tracked to signed clients, research searches excluded, bar rules respected. Flat fee.

Legal is the most expensive auction in Google Ads. Personal injury searches in Houston, Dallas or Phoenix average well over $100 a click, and family, immigration and employment searches run from $20 to $80 in most metros. At that price the difference between a firm that profits from Google Ads and one that does not is almost never the bid. It is what gets counted, what gets excluded and the page after the click.

## Where law firm accounts waste money

- Research searches billed as leads. "How much does a divorce cost", "can I sue for", "free legal advice", "statute of limitations". These match broad and phrase keywords, cost as much as a client search and almost never sign. Twelve months of search terms read line by line is the first task.

- One campaign for the whole firm. Family, immigration and personal injury share a budget, and the cheapest inquiries take it. Each practice area gets its own campaign, budget and landing page.

- A call counted as a client. Phone clicks and form fills are not signed clients. Call tracking tied to the keyword, intake software recording the outcome, and the case management system feeding back which inquiries became matters are what let Google optimize toward clients.

- The firm's homepage as the landing page. Someone who searched for an immigration attorney should land on a page about immigration law, with the attorney's name, the first step explained and the phone number at the top.

- Ads that would not pass the bar. Outcome claims, "specialist" where the state bar restricts the word, missing disclaimers. State bar advertising rules set what can be said, and the ads are written inside them.

## What a click costs by practice area and metro

Average cost per click from Google Ads keyword data for the US, October 2026, for the search with the city attached. Market averages, not a forecast.

| Search | Houston | Dallas | Phoenix |

| personal injury lawyer [city] | $126.93 | $139.57 | $126.26 |

At these prices, 100 clicks cost close to $13,000. If one in eight calls and one in three callers signs, that is about $3,100 per signed case before the fee. If a third of those clicks were research searches that should have been excluded, the real figure was closer to $2,100. That is the arithmetic the account is run on, and it is why the negatives program and the intake tracking come before any bidding change.

## What management includes for a law firm

- A campaign per practice area, with exact and phrase match, a negatives program built from the research vocabulary of each area, and location targeting matched to where the firm takes clients and is licensed.

- Measurement to the signed client. Call tracking, intake outcomes, and the case management system (Clio, MyCase, Filevine, Lawmatics or a spreadsheet) feeding back which inquiries opened a matter, imported to Google Ads as offline conversions. See conversion tracking.

- A page per practice area, built by me, with the attorney, the process, the fee basis, and a phone number and form that work on a phone at lunchtime. See landing pages.

- Local Services Ads alongside Search where the practice area qualifies, with the Google Screened process handled and the two channels compared on cost per signed client.

- Brand and competitor terms decided, not defaulted. Whether to bid on the firm's own name depends on who else is bidding on it; competitor bidding is permitted but usually poor value and in some states restricted. Both reviewed monthly.

- Microsoft Advertising once Google works: a professional audience on work devices, often at a lower cost per inquiry for legal searches. Microsoft Ads →

- A monthly report in signed clients and cost per signed client, by practice area, alongside the platform numbers so the two can be compared.

## Who this fits

US and Canadian firms from a few attorneys to mid-size regional practices, spending roughly $5,000 to $80,000 a month, in practice areas where a client is worth several thousand dollars or more: personal injury where the firm handles its own intake, family, immigration, employment, criminal defense, estate planning, business law. Lead resellers and mass-tort aggregators are not a fit. There is no law firm case on this site yet and none will be invented; the published cases show the method on other expensive auctions.

### FAQ

**How much should a law firm spend on Google Ads?** Enough to buy a meaningful number of clicks in your practice area and metro. At $30 to $140 a click, several thousand dollars a month is the floor for a single practice area in a large city, and personal injury needs more. The first call includes this arithmetic for your firm.

**Can you work within state bar advertising rules?** Yes. Ads avoid outcome claims and restricted terms, carry the disclaimers your state requires, and your compliance partner signs off the copy before it runs. Where a state requires ad filing or review, that is built into the timeline.

**Do you handle Local Services Ads?** Yes, where the practice area qualifies: the Google Screened process, the profile, the budget and the lead disputes, with LSA and Search compared on cost per signed client in the same report.

**Can you connect Google Ads to our case management system?** Yes, through an offline conversion import: Clio, MyCase, Filevine, Lawmatics and most systems can export the inquiries that became matters, and a scheduled upload teaches Google which clicks produced clients.

**How much does PPC management for a law firm cost?** A flat monthly fee set from the scope: practice areas, platforms and how much landing page and tracking work is included. Never a percentage of spend. Quoted in US dollars by email from the form. See pricing.

## Home Services PPC | Google Ads for HVAC, Plumbing & Contractors

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/home-services-ppc/
Description: Home services PPC: Google Ads and Local Services Ads for HVAC, plumbing, roofing and electrical, measured in booked jobs, by a consultant who has run HVAC and plumbing campaigns in Houston.

Contractors buy the most expensive local clicks outside legal: $30 to $55 for a plumber or AC repair search in the large Sun Belt metros. I have run Google Ads for an HVAC and plumbing company in Houston, one of those auctions. How I approach a contractor account is on this page.

## Where contractor accounts waste money

- Emergency and planned work in one campaign. "AC not cooling" at 9 pm in July and "new HVAC system cost" are different customers with different values. Sharing a budget, the cheap emergency clicks take it and the installs never get seen.

- A phone call counted as a job. Wrong numbers, suppliers, job seekers and existing customers all ring the tracked line. Until the office marks which calls were booked, Google optimizes toward whoever calls, not whoever buys.

- Service area set to the metro. A plumber in Katy paying for clicks from Baytown. Radius and ZIP targeting matched to the trucks' actual routes, with bids by area and hour.

- Local Services Ads ignored or left to run. Google Guaranteed leads are often cheaper than Search for emergency work and the two should be compared on cost per booked job, not run by different people.

- The homepage as the landing page. Someone with water on the floor needs the phone number, the response time and the service area in the first screen, not the company history.

## What a click costs by trade and metro

Average cost per click from Google Ads keyword data for the US, October 2026, for the search with the city attached. Market averages, not a forecast.

| Search | Houston | Dallas | Phoenix |

| plumber [city] | $35.53 | $35.66 | $54.16 |

| HVAC repair [city] | $29.18 | $43.67 | $17.70 |

| roofing company [city] | $14.44 | $10.66 | $16.74 |

The same trade costs very different amounts in neighboring markets: HVAC repair in Dallas costs two and a half times what it does in Phoenix, and a Phoenix plumber pays half as much again as a Houston one. Budgets set from a national average go wrong in both directions. An audit prices your own auction before anything is changed.

## How I run a contractor account

The order of work I follow in a home services account. The Houston engagement on results is described there without figures, because its data is confidential by contract.

- Campaigns split by type of job, so urgent, cheaper work does not absorb the budget meant for installs and higher-value repairs.

- Tracking that separates a booked job from a phone call, with the office marking call outcomes and the booked jobs fed back to Google.

- A weekly pass through the search terms, with a negatives list that grows every week, and steady tests of ads and landing pages.

- Bids by area and hour, matched to where the trucks go and to when emergency calls come in.

## What management includes for a contractor

- Google Search by service and urgency, Local Services Ads where the trade qualifies, and Microsoft Advertising once Google works, compared on cost per booked job.

- Call tracking with outcomes, the booking software (ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro, Jobber and others) feeding booked and completed jobs back as offline conversions. See conversion tracking.

- One page per service, built by me, with the phone number, the response time and the service area at the top, loading fast on a phone. See landing pages.

- Seasonal budgets planned in advance: cooling in May, heating in October, storm response when it happens.

- A monthly report in booked jobs and cost per booked job, by service line, alongside the platform numbers.

## Who this fits

HVAC, plumbing, electrical, roofing, garage door, pest control, restoration and similar contractors in the US and Canada, from a few trucks to regional multi-location companies, spending roughly $3,000 to $60,000 a month. Lead-generation networks that resell contractor leads are not a fit. For smaller budgets, see Google Ads for small business.

### FAQ

**How much should an HVAC or plumbing company spend on Google Ads?** Enough to buy a meaningful number of clicks at your metro's price: at $30 to $55 a click, a few thousand dollars a month is the floor for one trade in a large metro, and more during the season. The first call includes this arithmetic for your market.

**Do you manage Local Services Ads too?** Yes: the Google Guaranteed process, the profile, the budget, the lead disputes, and the comparison with Search on cost per booked job in the same report.

**Can you connect Google Ads to ServiceTitan or Housecall Pro?** Yes, through an offline conversion import: booked and completed jobs with their value exported from the booking software and uploaded on a schedule, so Google learns which clicks became jobs.

**Do you work with multi-location contractors?** Yes. Each location gets its own service area, budget and pages, with the shared structure maintained once, and the report broken down by location.

**How much does home services PPC management cost?** A flat monthly fee set from the scope: service lines, locations, platforms and how much landing page and tracking work is included. Never a percentage of spend. Quoted in US dollars by email from the form. See pricing.

## Where dental accounts waste money

- Health policy ignored. Google restricts personalized advertising on health conditions, so remarketing built on treatment pages is not available. The account has to work without it.

## What a click costs by metro

## Healthcare PPC | Google Ads for Clinics, Practices and Health Brands

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/healthcare-ppc/
Description: Healthcare PPC by an independent consultant: Google and Meta Ads for clinics and health brands, measured in booked appointments, within health policies.

Healthcare is a crowded auction with its own constraints: restricted remarketing, certification for some categories, claims the FTC and the platforms do not allow, HIPAA, and patients who research for weeks before booking. The accounts that work are the ones where the measurement reaches the appointment book and the campaigns respect the research journey instead of paying for it twice.

## What is different about healthcare accounts

- Policy limits the tools. Google restricts personalized advertising for health conditions, so remarketing lists built on condition pages are not available; some categories (prescription drugs, addiction treatment, certain procedures) require certification before ads run; Meta has its own health and wellness data restrictions. The structure has to work without the tools other sectors lean on.

- Claims are regulated. Outcome claims, before-and-after imagery for some procedures, and anything that implies a guarantee fall under the FTC and, for drugs and devices, the FDA. Copy is written inside those rules and your clinical or compliance lead signs it off.

- Research searches dominate. "Symptoms of", "is it normal", "does insurance cover" are expensive, well-meaning and do not book. They are excluded, and the budget goes to the searches that name a treatment, a provider type or a location.

- The conversion is an appointment, not a form. The front desk answers the phone; the scheduling system knows who attended. Until those feed back, Google optimizes toward whoever fills in a form, including the people who never show up.

- HIPAA shapes the measurement. No protected health information goes to the ad platforms. Conversions are outcomes, not diagnoses, and the setup is documented.

## What management includes

- Structure by service line and location. A campaign per service (orthopedics, fertility, dermatology, behavioral health, diagnostics, urgent care) with location targeting matched to how far patients travel for each, and the research vocabulary excluded.

- Measurement to the appointment. Call tracking with front-desk outcomes, the scheduling or practice management system feeding booked and attended appointments back as offline conversions, consent handled, and a privacy setup that keeps health data out of the ad platforms. See conversion tracking.

- Pages built for a worried person. One page per service with the provider, the process, insurance and cost answered, the next available appointment and a phone number at the top, loading fast on a phone. See landing pages.

- Meta where it fits. Awareness and remarketing for elective services, within Meta's health restrictions, judged on booked consultations rather than on form fills. Meta Ads →

- Reporting in appointments. Cost per booked and attended appointment by service line, alongside the platform numbers.

## Who this fits

US and Canadian clinics and practice groups, specialty practices, diagnostics and imaging, behavioral health providers working within the certification rules, med spas and aesthetics within the claims rules, and health brands selling direct. Typically $3,000 to $60,000 a month across Google and Meta. Healthcare and pharma are among the sectors I have worked in over 14 years; no patient-facing case is published on this site, and none will be invented. For dental practices specifically, see Google Ads for dentists.

### FAQ

**Can you run Google Ads for a clinic given the health policies?** Yes. The restrictions remove some tools (condition-based remarketing, some audience features) and require certification for certain categories, including addiction treatment and prescription drugs. The account is built to work within that, and the certification process is handled with you where it applies.

**How do you handle HIPAA?** No protected health information goes to Google or Meta. Conversions are sent as outcomes (booked, attended) with hashed contact data only where enhanced conversions are used; tags on pages that could reveal a condition are reviewed; and the setup is documented for your compliance officer. Where your counsel prefers server-side tagging with filtering, that is how it is built.

**Can you connect Google Ads to our scheduling system?** Usually, through an offline conversion import from the scheduling or practice management system, exporting which inquiries booked and attended without clinical data. Where there is no export, front-desk outcomes from call tracking do most of the job.

**Do you work with med spas and aesthetics?** Yes, within the claims rules: no outcome guarantees, before-and-after imagery only where the platform allows it, and copy signed off by your clinical lead.

**How much does healthcare PPC management cost?** A flat monthly fee set from the scope: service lines, locations, platforms and how much landing page and tracking work is included. Never a percentage of spend. Quoted in US dollars by email from the form. See pricing.

## SaaS PPC Consultant | Google Ads Measured in Pipeline and Payback

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/saas-ppc/
Description: SaaS PPC by an independent consultant: Google Ads connected to the CRM and reported in pipeline and CAC payback. Published B2B case with its limits.

Software companies have the cleanest data in paid media and often the worst use of it. The CRM knows which trials became customers and what they pay; the ad platforms are optimizing toward sign-ups. Connecting the two is most of the job, and it is where a SaaS account starts here.

## Where SaaS accounts leak

- Optimizing toward the top of the funnel. Free trials, demo requests and content downloads are easy to count and cheap to buy. Without product-qualified or sales-accepted stages flowing back, the platforms buy the cheapest sign-ups, which churn.

- Competitor and category terms treated the same. "[Competitor] alternative" and "best [category] software" bring different buyers at different stages and should sit in separate campaigns with separate pages and expectations.

- Brand taking the credit. Performance Max and broad match drift onto the brand name and the reported CAC looks wonderful. Brand is isolated, and the non-brand number is the one managed.

- Payback ignored. A customer acquired at $1,200 on a $49 monthly plan is a two-year payback before gross margin. The targets by plan and segment come from that arithmetic, not from a blended CAC.

## What management includes

- Measurement to the CRM. GA4 and Tag Manager with a user ID, HubSpot or Salesforce stages (MQL, SQL, opportunity, closed won, with amount) imported to Google Ads and Microsoft Advertising as offline conversions, so the platforms optimize toward revenue. See conversion tracking.

- Google Search by intent. Category, problem, integration and competitor campaigns, each with its own page and its own target, brand kept separate, Performance Max only with brand excluded and only once the conversion data deserves it.

- Microsoft Advertising for the professional audience on work devices, with LinkedIn profile bid adjustments Google cannot offer. Microsoft Ads →

- YouTube and Demand Gen for product demos and founder pieces, judged on the lift in branded search and on conversions, not on views. YouTube Ads →

- Pages per intent, built by me: comparison pages, integration pages, use-case pages, with the trial or demo form that asks the one qualifying question. See landing pages.

- Reporting in pipeline and payback. Qualified pipeline, closed-won revenue and CAC payback by channel and segment, alongside the platform numbers.

## A published SaaS result

At Pontomais, a time-tracking and HR software company in Brazil, I rebuilt the Google Ads account as an employee. Contact requests from Google Ads went from about five in a month to the hundreds over eight months, approximate volumes from my own experience on the project, and the full note is on results. The market was Brazil and the currency was different, but the method was the one above: the account rebuilt around buying intent, landing page changes, and daily feedback from sales on the quality of each contact. Intuit QuickBooks and Skillshare are among the subscription brands I have worked on in agency and in-house roles.

## Who this fits

B2B software companies in the US, Canada and anywhere that works in English, from seed to Series B or established vertical SaaS, spending roughly $5,000 to $80,000 a month on Google and Microsoft, with a CRM in use and a sales or product-led motion that can report stages. Consumer apps measured on installs are not a fit. For the wider B2B picture, see B2B PPC.

### FAQ

**What CAC should a SaaS company expect from Google Ads?** No honest number exists before the account and the CRM are read together. What is measurable from the first month is CAC by channel and segment against your plan prices, which gives payback, and that is the figure the targets are set from.

**Can you connect Google Ads to HubSpot or Salesforce?** Yes. Offline conversion import from CRM stages with amounts, enhanced conversions for leads, and a user ID in GA4 so the journey from click to closed won is visible. The setup is documented so your RevOps team owns it.

**Should we bid on competitor names?** Usually yes, in a separate campaign with its own page and a target that reflects the lower conversion rate. Comparison pages that are honest about where the competitor is better convert well and stay within the advertising rules.

**Do you run product-led growth accounts?** Yes, provided product-qualified signals (activation, team invites, usage thresholds) can be fed back. Without them the platforms optimize toward sign-ups that never activate, and the budget is better spent elsewhere.

**How much does SaaS PPC management cost?** A flat monthly fee set from the scope: platforms, markets, campaigns and how much landing page and tracking work is included. Never a percentage of spend. Quoted in US dollars, pounds or euros by email from the form. See pricing.

## PPC Consultant Houston | Google Ads With a Published Houston Case

Independent PPC consultant for Houston companies: 14+ years running Google, Microsoft and Meta Ads, Houston HVAC and plumbing experience, calls on Central time, and a fee that does not carry a Galleria office inside it.

## What Houston accounts usually need

Houston is the fourth-largest metro in the country and one of the most spread out: a service business in Katy, Sugar Land, The Woodlands and Pearland is running four different auctions, not one. Energy, healthcare, legal and the trades all buy paid search seriously, and the summer makes home services one of the most expensive local markets in the United States.

- Location targeting that matches the map. The metro is eight counties and a 60-mile drive across. ZIP and radius targeting matched to where you actually serve, with bids by area and hour, instead of one pin downtown.

- Inquiry quality over inquiry count. Call tracking tied to the keyword, forms that qualify, and the CRM or booking software feeding back which inquiries became customers, so bidding learns from revenue.

- A landing page per service. Not the homepage, and not one contact page for twelve services.

- Season planned in advance. Cooling budgets in May, storm response when it happens, and the quieter months used for installs and planned work.

## What a click costs in Houston compared with other metros

Average cost per click for the same search with the city name attached, from Google Ads keyword data for the US, October 2026. Market averages, not a forecast for your account.

| Search | Houston | Dallas | Phoenix |

| plumber [city] | $35.53 | $35.66 | $54.16 |

| HVAC repair [city] | $29.18 | $43.67 | $17.70 |

| roofing company [city] | $14.44 | $10.66 | $16.74 |

Houston is not the most expensive metro for everything: HVAC repair costs a third less than in Dallas, and a plumber click costs far less than in Phoenix. IT support is the outlier, at more than twice the Dallas price. The lesson is to price your own auction rather than assume, which is one of the first things an audit does.

## The Houston HVAC and plumbing engagement

An HVAC and plumbing company in Houston, Google Ads and Performance Max from May 2025 to February 2026. Its performance data is confidential under my contract, so no figures are published, and the write-up is on results. How I approach that kind of account:

- A weekly pass through the search terms and steady tests of ads and landing pages.

For a Houston law firm or clinic the same three moves apply: separate the practice areas or service lines sharing one campaign, count a signed client or an attended appointment rather than a call, and cut the research searches that eat budget at the prices in the table. Home services PPC →

## Google Ads Consultation | One-Off PPC Session With Written Notes

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/google-ads-consultation/
Description: Book a Google Ads consultation: one working session on your account with a senior independent consultant, written notes afterwards. Fixed price.

Not every account needs an audit or a retainer. Sometimes a business needs a senior person to look at the account for an hour, answer the three questions that have been going around for months, and write down what to do next. That is the consultation, and it is the smallest way to work with me.

## When a consultation is the right size

- A decision is pending. Whether to move to Performance Max, whether to take the agency's proposal, whether the budget increase is justified, whether to bid on the brand. A second opinion from someone with no retainer to win.

- An in-house marketer wants a senior check. You run the account yourself and want an experienced pair of eyes on the structure, the tracking and the search terms before the next quarter.

- Something broke. Conversions stopped recording, the account was suspended, spend doubled overnight, and you need the cause and the fix without a six-week engagement.

- You are choosing a vendor. You have two agency proposals and want them read by someone who runs accounts, with the questions to ask each one.

## How the consultation works

- Before the call. You send the form with the spend band, the platforms and the questions. If the account is live, read-only access to Google Ads and GA4 so the hour is spent on answers rather than on screen-sharing.

- The session. A video call of about an hour, in a US morning or early afternoon, working through the account and your questions in order of money at stake. Recorded if you want it.

- Written notes within two working days. What was found, what to do, in what order, and what to measure to know it worked. Written so your team or your agency can act on it.

- Credited if it grows. If the consultation becomes a full audit or management within 60 days, the consultation fee is credited against it.

## Google Ads Audit Example | What I Check Before Recommending More Budget

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/google-ads-audit-example/
Description: A worked Google Ads audit on an illustrative account: the eight checks, what each one found, and why the answer was to fix three things before adding budget.

Most audits are a list of 60 findings sorted by nothing. This page walks through the eight checks I run, in the order I run them, on one illustrative account, and ends where a real audit ends: a short list of what to fix first and whether more budget would help.

This account is illustrative. It is a composite built to show the method, and the figures are invented for the example, not taken from a client. The checks, the order and the kind of findings are the ones I see in real accounts.

## The example account

A home services company in a mid-sized US metro: about $8,000 a month on Google Ads, one Search campaign and one Performance Max campaign, managed by an agency for two years. The owner's question: "Leads are flat. Should we double the budget?"

## The eight checks, in order

### 1. Conversion tracking: what is being counted

What I look at: every conversion action, which ones are primary, how each is triggered, and whether the numbers match what the office actually received.

Found: four primary actions, including a page view of /contact/ and a click on the phone number. The account reported 310 conversions last month; the office logged about 120 real inquiries.

Why it matters: the bidding was optimizing toward people opening the contact page. Every other number in the account inherits this error, so it is fixed first.

### 2. Search terms: what people actually typed

What I look at: 90 days of search terms, sorted by cost, not by clicks.

Found: 22% of spend on terms like "hvac technician salary", "how to fix ac yourself" and a competitor's brand name.

Why it matters: that is money with no buyer behind it. Negatives and tighter match types recover it without touching the budget.

### 3. Match types and structure

Found: almost everything on broad match, in one ad group per campaign, so emergency repair, installation and maintenance shared one ad and one landing page.

Why it matters: different jobs, different value, same bid. Splitting by type of job is what lets the budget go to the work that pays.

### 4. Performance Max and the brand

Found: Performance Max took 41% of the budget, and a large share of its conversions came from people searching the company's own name.

Why it matters: those customers were coming anyway. The campaign looked like the best performer because it was collecting brand traffic. Brand exclusion first, then judge it.

### 5. Locations and hours

Found: "presence or interest" location targeting, so clicks came from people outside the service area, and ads ran overnight with nobody to answer.

Why it matters: both are settings, not strategy, and both are quick to fix.

### 6. The page after the click, and the phone

Found: ads sent everyone to the homepage; on a phone, the first screen had no number and no form. Test calls at lunchtime went to voicemail twice in five tries.

Why it matters: no bid change fixes a page that does not answer the search, or a call nobody picks up. See landing pages.

### 7. Lead quality, from the CRM or the office

Found: the agency reported cost per conversion; nobody had compared leads to booked jobs. The office estimated one in four calls was a job.

Why it matters: until booked jobs are fed back, the account cannot learn which searches bring customers. See conversion tracking.

### 8. Budget and impression share

Found: the Search campaign lost about 30% of impression share to budget, but most of the budget was going to the waste found in checks 2, 4 and 5.

Why it matters: this is the check that answers the owner's question.

## The verdict

Do not double the budget yet. Fix three things first: count only real inquiries (check 1), cut the waste in search terms and brand traffic (checks 2 and 4), and send ads to a page that works on a phone, with a phone that gets answered (check 6). In an account like this, that work usually frees enough spend to fill the lost impression share without adding a dollar. Budget becomes the right question after six to eight weeks of clean data.

## What the written audit contains

- Findings ranked by impact, each with the evidence (screenshots or exports) and the fix.

- The three things to do first, in order, and who should do them.

- What not to change yet, and why.

- A short answer to the question you came with, such as "should we spend more?".

The account stays yours; read-only access is all an audit needs. See Google Ads audit for scope and delivery, or a Google Ads consultation for a one-off working session.

### FAQ

**How long does an audit like this take?** Five to seven business days from read-only access, depending on how many campaigns and how much history there is.

**Do I need to give you access?** Read-only access to Google Ads and GA4 is enough. Nothing is changed in the account during the audit.

**What if the account is in good shape?** Then the audit says so, explains why, and the answer to "should we spend more?" may simply be yes, with where to put it.

Visitors in the EEA, the UK and Switzerland see a cookie banner, and nothing is stored on their device until they accept; if they reject, the tags run in cookieless mode. Elsewhere the tags run by default.

You can block these with your browser's tracking protection or an extension such as Google's Analytics opt-out; the site works the same without them.

## Google Ads for Housing, Jobs or Credit: What You Can't Target in the US

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/guides/google-ads-housing-employment-credit/
Description: Google Ads rules for housing, employment and credit ads in the US and Canada: which targeting is off limits, what still works, and how to fix an affected campaign.

If you sell or rent homes, recruit, or offer loans or credit cards, Google applies a separate set of targeting rules to your ads in the United States and Canada. The rules date from October 2020, but they still catch real estate agents, mortgage brokers, staffing firms and lenders who copy a campaign from another business or let an agency apply a standard audience setup. This guide sets out what Google restricts, what you can still use, and what to change today.

Messages this guide covers: Housing in personalized advertising, Employment in personalized advertising, Consumer finance in personalized advertising, Restricted targeting, Policy Manager.

## Who the rules apply to

Google groups these businesses under "Access to opportunities categories (US and Canada only)" in its personalized advertising policy. Enforcement follows where the ads are shown, not where you are based. Google's FAQ on the policy says: "The focus of the enforcement will be on ad target geo location and not based on advertiser's billing or physical location."

| Category | Google's description | Restricted examples | Not restricted, per Google's FAQ |

| Housing | "homes for sale or rental ... as well as products or services enabling the sale or rental of homes" (housing page) | Listing sites, a single home for sale, real estate agents or brokers | Hotels and vacation rentals, office space, property management services |

| Employment | "employment opportunities or hiring a person for a job" (employment page) | Job ads, recruitment and job listing sites, freelance or gig job listings | Career advice, employment training, networking services |

| Consumer finance (credit) | "offers relating to credit, banking products and services, or certain financial planning and management services" (consumer finance page) | Credit cards and loans, including home and car loans | Financial guidance, gift cards |

One detail has moved since 2020. The original FAQ listed checking accounts as not restricted, while Google's current consumer finance page lists "Banking and checking accounts" as an example in scope. Treat banking products as in scope.

You do not declare the category yourself. Google's FAQ says it reviews "both the ad text and landing page", and for Display and YouTube ads the visual elements too.

## The five targeting options you can't use

Google's policy pages for all three categories list the same five for the United States and Canada: gender, age, parental status, marital status and ZIP codes. In practice, per Google's FAQ:

- Age, gender and parental status must target everyone, and bid adjustments on them must be "reverted to 0% or removed".

- Detailed demographics for marital status and parental status must be removed.

- The life event "Marriage", including getting married soon and recently married, must be removed.

- ZIP code targeting must be removed. In Canada the full postal code is out, but Google says the first three characters (the FSA) are acceptable.

- Customer Match and remarketing lists are only affected "if they use demographics, Marriage/Marital Status, Parental status, or ZIP Code signals to build users lists."

## What still works

From Google's policy pages: "Targeting geographic locations using radius, as well as city and country-based targeting is allowed. Radius targeting requires setting at least 1 km around any given location."

Google's FAQ lists as not restricted: household income, homeownership status, education, in-market and affinity segments, custom segments, life events other than marriage, and city, county, DMA and radius targeting.

Keywords are not part of these rules. A Search campaign built on what people type, such as "homes for sale in Plano", "CDL driver jobs Dallas" or "refinance rates", remains the cleanest way to reach buyers in these categories.

## Why this matters for the business, not only for compliance

- A ZIP code list is the most common casualty. Agents and lenders often target the ten ZIP codes they know best. Rebuild the same map with a radius around each neighborhood, or with city and county targeting.

- Age targeting is the second. A senior living community or a first-time buyer program cannot narrow by age in Google Ads. The precision has to come from keywords and from landing pages written for that buyer.

- Ads stop, and so do new campaigns. Google's FAQ says ads using the restricted targeting "will stop serving", and that an account cannot create new campaigns until the policy has been accepted.

## What to do today

- Open Policy Manager in Google Ads. Google's FAQ says "Impacted ads will be included in the Policy Manager page of your Google Ads account."

- Fix the audiences. In each campaign that advertises homes, jobs or credit, set age, gender and parental status to all, and remove marital and parental detailed demographics and the Marriage life event.

- Fix the locations. Replace ZIP codes with a radius of at least 1 km, cities or counties.

- Check your lists. If a Customer Match or remarketing list was built from age, gender, marital status or ZIP code, stop using it in these campaigns.

- Let the ad be reviewed again. Google: "Your ad will be automatically reviewed again." Check the status in "Ads & assets".

- Move the precision into keywords and pages. That is where it now lives. A Google Ads audit covers this in one pass if several campaigns are affected.

A longer guide to real estate campaigns, including this policy, is on diwizi.com.

## Official sources used in this guide

- https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/143465?hl=en
- https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/16701755
- https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/16700442
- https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/16700846
- https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/9917652?hl=en
- https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/9997418?hl=en

### FAQ

**Do these rules apply if my business is based outside the US?** Yes, if the ads target people in the United States or Canada. Google's FAQ says enforcement is based on where the ad is targeted, not on the advertiser's billing or physical location.

**Can I still target my city with housing or loan ads?** Yes. Google allows city, county and DMA targeting and a radius of at least 1 km. ZIP code targeting is not allowed for these ads in the US, and full postal codes are not allowed in Canada.

**Is a property management company affected?** Google's FAQ lists property management services as not restricted and promoting homes for sale or rental as restricted. If your ads promote specific rentals, assume the rules apply.

**Are keywords restricted for housing, job or credit ads?** No. The restrictions cover demographics, the Marriage life event, lists built from those signals and ZIP codes. Keyword targeting is not part of them, which makes Search campaigns the most precise option left.

**Does Meta have the same rule?** Meta has its own Special Ad Categories for housing, employment and credit, with similar limits. This guide covers Google only.


---

## Do US Websites Need a Cookie Banner for Google Ads? CCPA Explained

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/guides/google-ads-us-privacy-laws/
Description: US privacy laws and Google Ads: when the CCPA applies to a business, the Do Not Sell or Share link, Global Privacy Control and Google's restricted data processing.

Owners who see European cookie banners everywhere often assume a US site needs one too before Google Ads or GA4 can run. California's privacy law works differently: it is mostly an opt-out law, and it only applies to businesses above certain thresholds. This guide sets out who the CCPA covers, what it asks of a business that advertises, and what Google offers to help, quoting the official pages. It is not legal advice: if you are near the thresholds, ask a lawyer.

Messages this guide covers: Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information, Global Privacy Control, Restricted data processing, restricted_data_processing, Consent mode.

## Does the CCPA apply to your business?

The California Privacy Protection Agency's FAQ says the CCPA applies to for-profit businesses that do business in California and meet any of these thresholds:

- "Have a gross annual revenue of $26.625 million or more (effective January 1, 2025) for the preceding calendar year"

- "Buy, sell, or share the personal information of 100,000 or more California residents or households"

- "Derive 50% or more of their annual revenue from selling or sharing California residents' personal information"

The California Attorney General's CCPA page still shows the original $25 million figure. The agency's FAQ has the adjusted one. The Attorney General's page also says the CCPA "generally does not apply to nonprofit organizations or government agencies".

For most small businesses running Google Ads, none of the three applies. If you are close to one of them, the rest of this guide is the part to read with your lawyer.

## Why advertising counts: "sale" and "sharing"

The Attorney General's page explains that "sharing refers specifically to sharing for cross-context behavioral advertising, which is the targeting of advertising to a consumer based on the consumer's personal information obtained from the consumer's online activity across numerous websites."

In Google Ads terms, that is remarketing and audience lists built from what people did on your site and elsewhere. Showing a Search ad to someone who typed a query is a different thing. So the question for a business covered by the CCPA is not whether it uses Google Ads, but whether it uses data from your site to target people across other sites.

## Opt-out, not a cookie banner

The CCPA gives California residents a "right to opt-out of sale or sharing", including "via a user-enabled global privacy control". It does not require opt-in consent before cookies are set. The opt-in requirement on the Attorney General's page is for minors: businesses "can only sell the personal information of a child that they know to be under the age of 16 if they get affirmative authorization ('opt-in')".

A covered business that sells or shares personal information must offer:

- A "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information" link. The Attorney General describes "a clear and conspicuous" link on the website, and says businesses "cannot require you to create an account" to use it. The same link must appear in the privacy policy.

- Respect for Global Privacy Control. Consumers "can also submit an opt-out request via a user-enabled global privacy control, like the GPC". A browser with GPC switched on is an opt-out.

- A 12-month wait before asking again. "Businesses must wait at least 12 months before asking you to opt back in to the sale or sharing of your personal information."

This is enforced. In August 2022 the Attorney General announced a $1.2 million settlement with Sephora, which had allowed third-party tracking on its site and, according to the Attorney General, failed to process opt-out requests "via user-enabled global privacy controls".

## What Google offers: restricted data processing

Google's restricted data processing page describes a mode in which "Google restricts the way it uses certain unique identifiers", acting as your service provider under its US state privacy terms. What changes for the advertiser:

- Remarketing stops for those users. "Certain features will be unavailable, including adding users to remarketing lists."

- Measurement keeps working. "Even when restricted data processing is enabled, features, such as conversion tracking and campaign measurement, will continue to function as normal."

- Two ways to switch it on in Google Ads. A "restricted_data_processing" parameter in the Google tag for particular users, such as people who clicked your opt-out link, or a checkbox in the remarketing tag settings for all users in applicable US states.

- GPC is handled for you in some states. Google says it "will turn off ads targeting and activate restrictive data processing (RDP) if we receive a GPC in these U.S. States."

- A California exception. "As of July 1, 2023, restricted data processing is not available in California where the advertiser engages in cross-context behavioral advertising, including Customer Match."

Google's US state privacy page adds that "Advertisers should work with their legal advisors to determine whether and how they should comply with applicable US state privacy laws."

Consent mode is a separate tool. Google's consent mode page says it "lets you communicate your users' cookie or app identifier consent status to Google" and "doesn't provide a consent banner or widget". In advanced mode Google defaults to a consented state unless a choice is made, "though there may be regional behavioral differences for specific areas like the EEA, Switzerland, and the UK". If your ads also reach Europe or the UK, those visitors need a consent banner, and the UK rules are covered on ppcconsultancy.uk.

## What to do today

- Check the three thresholds. Revenue, the number of California residents or households whose data you buy, sell or share, and the share of revenue from selling or sharing. If none applies, the CCPA does not apply, and you do not need a California opt-out link for it.

- List what your tags do. Conversion tracking and Search ads are one thing. Remarketing, Customer Match and audience lists are the "sharing" the law is about.

- If you are covered: add the "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information" link to the site and the privacy policy, make it work without an account, and make sure your consent tool honors GPC.

- Connect the opt-out to Google. Set the restricted_data_processing parameter for users who opt out, or enable it for all users in applicable states. Conversion tracking keeps working either way.

- If you advertise to Europe or the UK, run a consent banner for those visitors, separately from the US setup.

- Have the setup checked once. A conversion tracking setup covers the tags, consent signals and restricted data processing together.

A wider look at how privacy changes affect paid media in 2026 is on diwizi.com.

## Official sources used in this guide

- https://cppa.ca.gov/faq.html
- https://oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa
- https://oag.ca.gov/news/press-releases/attorney-general-bonta-announces-settlement-sephora-part-ongoing-enforcement
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/9614122?hl=en
- https://business.safety.google/usaprivacy/
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/10000067?hl=en

Housing, jobs and credit adsThe five targeting options Google bans for home, job and credit ads in the US and Canada, what still works, and how to fix an affected campaign.Local Services Ads verificationThe Google Verified badge, background checks, license and insurance documents, how long verification takes and why verified ads still get no leads.All guides

### FAQ

**Do US websites need a cookie banner for Google Ads?** Not under the CCPA in the way European sites do. The CCPA is an opt-out law: businesses it covers must offer a Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information link and honor Global Privacy Control. Opt-in is required for selling the data of minors under 16. Other states have their own laws, so check with a lawyer if you are close to the thresholds.

**Does the CCPA apply to small businesses?** Only if they meet one of three thresholds: gross annual revenue of $26.625 million or more (as adjusted from January 1, 2025), buying, selling or sharing the personal information of 100,000 or more California residents or households, or deriving 50% or more of revenue from selling or sharing it.

**Is Google Ads remarketing a sale or sharing of data?** Under the CCPA, sharing means sharing for cross-context behavioral advertising, which targets ads based on activity across websites. Remarketing and audience lists built from site visitors fall into that description. Search ads shown to people who typed a query do not depend on it.

**Does conversion tracking stop if I enable restricted data processing?** No. Google says conversion tracking and campaign measurement continue to function as normal. What stops is adding those users to remarketing lists.

**What is Global Privacy Control?** A browser setting that signals the user's choice to opt out. The California Attorney General treats it as a valid opt-out request, and in 2022 settled with Sephora for $1.2 million partly for not processing it.


---

## Local Services Ads Verification Stuck? What Google Checks and How Long

URL: https://googleadsfreelancer.com/guides/local-services-ads-verification/
Description: Local Services Ads verification in the US: the Google Verified badge, background checks, license and insurance documents, how long it takes and why ads stop showing.

Local Services Ads put your business above the regular Google ads, with a badge and a call button, and you pay per lead instead of per click. Before any of that, every business has to pass Google's screening and verification, and that is where most owners get stuck: a name that does not match, an insurance certificate about to expire, a technician who never finished a background check. This guide follows Google's own help pages step by step.

Messages this guide covers: Google Verified, Business Verification, Proof of Insurance, Background check, Business Profile, Suspended.

## First: the badge changed

Google has replaced the old Google Guaranteed and Google Screened badges with one badge. On its Google Verified badge page, Google says it is "simplifying our advertiser badging by launching a single badge for all advertisers". New advertisers "will need to successfully complete the Local Services screening and verification process in order to get the Google Verified badge", and existing advertisers "will automatically earn the new Google Verified badge".

The money-back guarantee is gone. Google "will be discontinuing the Money Back Guarantee associated with the Google Guarantee badge". Reimbursement requests only apply to services booked through Local Services Ads before December 7, 2025, and must be submitted within 30 days of the service. If a competitor or an old article promises customers a Google guarantee, it is out of date.

## What Google checks

Google's screening and verification page: "all businesses must pass Google's screening and verification process. The process varies by business category and location." Your dashboard shows which checks apply to you. In the US they can include:

| Check | What Google asks for | Where owners get stuck |

| Google Business Profile | The person completing the checks must own or manage the matched profile | A former agency or employee owns the profile. Google says this step can take up to 24 hours to show as done. |

| Business registration | Your D-U-N-S number, or else Secretary of State registration, an EIN from the IRS, or Department of Revenue registration | No D-U-N-S number yet. Google notes the application can take up to 30 days. |

| Business representative | An identity check by Google's partner Evident, with "a clear unexpired government-issued photo ID" | The representative's name and the legal business name are not an exact match. |

| Background checks | All owners, plus every worker "who will perform core services for the customer", including contractors and temporary workers | One technician never completes it. Google says office staff and customer support "don't need to complete background checks". |

| Licenses | State-level licenses for your category, which Google "validates ... against the state or country databases" | The license is under a different name, or has expired. |

| Insurance | Proof of insurance with a policy number | The name, address or coverage amount does not match, or the document expires within 14 days. |

Per Google, background checks cost the business nothing and do not involve a credit check. In the US they include identity and criminal history checks and cross-checks against national sex offender, terrorist and sanctions registries. The category-by-category list of insurance and license requirements is on Google's US requirements page.

## How long it takes

Google's US requirements page: "On average, this process takes 3–4 weeks to complete after submitting your documents." Add up to 30 days if you still need a D-U-N-S number.

If a background check fails, Google says the business must wait 30 days to reapply, and 180 days after a second denial. That is the strongest reason to check every name and document before you submit.

Some US advertisers are asked for extra, risk-based verification after they start. Google gives them 14 days to complete the additional steps "to keep their ad serving".

## Insurance documents that pass

From Google's guidelines for North America:

- "The document must be active and valid for at least 14 days after the time of submission."

- "The name on the documentation must match the name you want to advertise with."

- "A policy number must be displayed."

- "The business address listed must cover the service area you want to advertise in."

- "The insurance amount must be equal to or greater than the amount required" for your category.

- "The document must be legitimate and non-editable."

Per Google's upload instructions, documents go in the dashboard under Business Verification: next to Proof of Insurance, click Submit document. Licenses are added with Add details: business name, license number and expiration date.

## Verified, but no leads?

Google's list of reasons Local Services Ads don't run, with what to check:

- The account is inactive or the ad is off. The ad must be toggled on, and Google says if "you're listed as not taking customers, your ad won't show".

- Account or billing issues. "Your ads won't run until these issues are resolved."

- Budget. Your monthly budget is your average daily budget multiplied by 30.4. A small budget means few leads.

- Settings that are too narrow. "Overly restrictive settings may prevent your ads from being shown", for example a small service area or few job types.

- Reviews. Google's ranking page: "serious or repeatedly negative customer feedback may result in lower rankings (including not showing at all)."

- Suspension. Google sends an in-account and an email notice, and accounts related to a suspended one may be suspended too, per its suspension page.

- Missed re-verification. Google warns it "may result in the loss of their badge, a pause on their ads, or account suspension".

## What to do today

- List the open checks. Open the Local Services dashboard and write down every check that is not done.

- Make the name identical everywhere. Google Business Profile, D-U-N-S, license, insurance and the name you advertise with.

- Check the insurance dates. Renew first if the certificate expires within the next month.

- Chase the background checks. Send the link to every owner and every field worker, and keep a list of who has finished.

- Put renewals in the calendar. Each license and insurance renewal date, so the badge is not lost later.

- Once verified, answer leads the same day. And ask for reviews: ranking depends on them.

How Local Services Ads compare with regular Search ads, and how to track their calls, is covered on diwizi.com: Local Services Ads vs Google Search Ads and call tracking for Local Services Ads. For home service businesses running both, see home services PPC.

### FAQ

**Is Local Services Ads the same as Google Ads?** No. It is a separate product with its own dashboard, paid per lead rather than per click. Many home service businesses run both, because regular Search ads cover searches and services Local Services Ads does not.

**How long does Local Services Ads verification take?** Three to four weeks on average after you submit your documents, according to Google's US requirements page, plus up to 30 days for a D-U-N-S number if you do not have one.

**Does my office manager need a background check?** No. Google says office managers, clerical workers and customer support staff who don't service customers directly don't need one. Owners and every worker who performs the service do.

**Is there still a Google Guarantee for my customers?** No. Google discontinued the money-back guarantee when it moved to the single Google Verified badge. Services booked before December 7, 2025 could still be claimed within 30 days of the service.

**What happens if a background check fails?** Google says the business must wait 30 days to reapply, and 180 days after a second denial. Check names and documents carefully before submitting.
